John Whitmer’s heading links the revelation to that offer, though later histories tie it to excesses among new converts. The revelation also named Edward Partridge bishop, the first known use of that title in the Church.
passages.summary: The revelation addresses the elders as people the Lord delights to bless. It commands them to assemble and agree on his word. By the prayer of faith they will receive his law to govern the Church. Whoever receives the law and does it is a disciple; whoever claims it but does not is not. It says Joseph should have a house built in which to live and translate. Sidney Rigdon may live as he thinks best while he keeps the commandments. Edward Partridge is to be appointed by the Church’s voice and ordained a bishop. He is to leave his business, for his heart is pure like Nathanael’s, a man without guile.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 41–44 uses verses 1–6 to ask how disciples prepare to receive the Lord’s law. Verse 2 tells the elders to “agree upon my word” before the law comes; why might agreement come first?

contextNote.title: What makes someone a disciple
contextNote.text: The Kirtland converts had gone months without settled leaders or rules. Verses 2–3 promise a law that will show “how to govern my church.” Verse 5 sets the test before the law even arrives. A disciple is one who “receiveth my law and doeth it.” Claiming the law without doing it marks a person as “not my disciple.” Verse 6 gives the reason, since holy things should not go to the unworthy. In this passage, discipleship is measured by doing, not by professing.

passages.title: The law of the Church joins mission, morals, and consecration
passages.setting: Joseph Smith had reached Kirtland, Ohio, only days earlier, and many new converts were waiting for direction. Earlier revelations had promised that the law would be given once the Saints gathered in Ohio. On 9 February 1831 twelve elders met, prayed together, and asked practical questions about gathering, governance, and property. Joseph dictated verses 1–72 in their presence. The Joseph Smith Papers date verses 74–93 to 23 February, when Joseph and seven elders asked how to apply the law.
passages.summary: The revelation calls itself a law and first sends every elder except Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon to preach two by two. Edward Partridge keeps his office, and no one may preach unless ordained by someone with known authority. Teachers are to teach from the Bible and the Book of Mormon, and only by the Spirit. Then it gives moral laws against killing, stealing, lying, lust, adultery, and speaking evil. It commands the Saints to consecrate property to the bishop for the poor, each becoming a steward of what he receives. Surplus goes to a storehouse for the needy, for lands, and for building the New Jerusalem. It adds rules on plain dress, idleness, care for the sick, and seeking revelation. The later verses set procedures for church discipline and for handing crimes to the law of the land.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 41–44 uses verses 30–42 to show how early Saints cared for those in need. Verse 38 says serving “the least of these” is serving Christ; how could verses 40–42 shape your own use of time and money?

contextNote.title: Consecration as a way to remember the poor
contextNote.text: The elders had asked how to provide for families and for members coming from New York. Verse 30 answers with a command to “remember the poor” and consecrate property for their support. It binds the gift “with a covenant and a deed which cannot be broken.” Verse 32 then returns to each giver a stewardship sufficient for his family. Verse 38 gives the reason behind the system: what is done for “the least of these” is done for Christ. In this passage, consecration is a legal transfer of property joined to a religious covenant.

passages.title: Only one man is appointed to receive revelations for the Church
passages.setting: In February 1831 Joseph Smith was newly settled in Kirtland, Ohio. The Ohio converts had gone months without experienced leaders. A woman remembered as Mrs. Hubble, probably Louisa Hubbell, claimed to receive commandments for the Church, and some members believed her. Joseph inquired of the Lord, and this revelation was the reply. The Joseph Smith Papers date it between 9 February and the end of the month.
passages.summary: The revelation tells the elders they have received a law through the one appointed to receive revelations. No one else is appointed to that gift while he abides in the Lord. If it is taken from him, his only power is to appoint another in his place. The elders are not to accept anyone else’s teachings as revelations. When assembled, they are to instruct and edify each other and sanctify themselves. They are to uphold Joseph and provide his food and clothing. Then it turns to the coming day of the Lord, when thunders, lightnings, and God’s voice call the nations to repent. It describes the Millennium, Satan bound, and the earth passing away, and ends, “Be sober.”

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 41–44 uses verses 1–16 to teach that God guides his Church through his prophet. Verses 8–9 tell members to “instruct and edify each other”; how does that fit with verse 3’s single channel for revelation?

contextNote.title: One channel for commandments
contextNote.text: Members in Kirtland were hearing a woman announce new commandments, and some accepted them. Verse 3 answers that there is “none other appointed unto you” to receive commandments and revelations. Verse 5 turns that into a rule: do not receive others’ teachings as revelations. Verse 6 gives the purpose, “that you may not be deceived.” The appointment is conditional, since it lasts only “if he abide in me.” In this passage, being appointed means holding a single, recognized office for revelation to the whole Church.

passages.title: Gather the elders, convert many, and organize under the law
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, in the latter part of February 1831. It is addressed to Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon. A letter Joseph wrote to Martin Harris on 22 February seems to allude to it, so it likely came before that date. The Church later set a conference for early June 1831, which Joseph’s history links to this call.
passages.summary: The revelation says the elders should be called together from every direction, by letter or other means. If they are faithful, the Spirit will be poured out when they assemble. They will then preach repentance in the nearby regions. Many will be converted, giving the Saints power to organize under the laws of man. That organization will protect them from enemies and help them keep God’s laws. Finally the elders must visit the poor and needy and relieve them until all is done by the law.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 41–44 presents these revelations as the Lord’s law to govern his Church. Verse 2 ties the outpouring of the Spirit to the elders gathering in faith; what does verse 6 add about what that gathering is for?

contextNote.title: Why organize by the laws of man
contextNote.text: The young Church in Ohio held property and cared for the poor, and verse 5 says it had enemies. Verse 4 links growth to a practical step: enough converts would let the Saints organize “according to the laws of man.” Verse 5 gives the reasons. Such organization would keep enemies from having power over them and help them keep God’s laws. Verse 6 sets a duty beside it: relief of “the poor and the needy.” In this passage, organizing under the laws of man means using civil forms to protect the Church’s work, not replacing God’s law.

passages.title: Signs of Christ’s coming are promises kept, not reasons for fear
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Kirtland, Ohio, around 7 March 1831. Two early copies date it 6 March instead. His later history says false newspaper reports were then circulating to discourage interest in the Church. He described the revelation as a source of joy to the Saints. It is addressed to the whole Church.
passages.summary: The revelation opens with the voice of the Creator calling the Church to listen. It presents Christ as an advocate pleading with the Father for those who believe. It then repeats what Jesus told his disciples about the coming fall of the Jerusalem temple. It describes wars, sickness, earthquakes, and a gospel light that many reject. The disciples are told not to be troubled, and a fig tree parable shows how to read the signs. It describes Christ’s return, the Jews seeing his wounds, and the wise who abide the day. It then tells Joseph to translate the New Testament. Finally, it calls the elders to gather west and build the New Jerusalem, a city of refuge called Zion.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for section 45, “The Promises … Shall Be Fulfilled,” reads these signs as reasons for hope in Christ. According to verses 32 and 57, what helps disciples “stand in holy places” and avoid deception?

contextNote.title: Signs given to steady, not to frighten
contextNote.text: Verses 26–33 list wars, sickness, earthquakes, and failing hearts. A list like that could easily cause alarm. Verse 34 says the disciples who first heard it “were troubled.” Verse 35 answers that fear directly: these same events show that the promises will be fulfilled. Verses 37–38 add the fig tree, whose tender leaves mean summer is near. Verse 57 then names who will “abide the day”: those who took the Holy Spirit for their guide. In this passage, a sign marks a promise coming due, not only a danger.

passages.title: Gifts of the Spirit are given so that all may benefit
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Kirtland, Ohio, around 8 March 1831. The day in the earliest copy is hard to read but is probably the 8th. Members had begun keeping unbelievers out of their meetings, and some questioned the practice. Joseph had also met spiritual displays in the Ohio branches that he judged unsound. The revelation addressed both concerns for the whole Church.
passages.summary: The revelation says elders should lead meetings as the Holy Spirit directs. It forbids casting anyone out of public meetings. Earnest seekers who are not members may stay in sacrament and confirmation meetings. Members who have sinned should not take the sacrament until they make reconciliation. It warns against deception and tells members to “seek ye earnestly the best gifts.” It then lists gifts of the Spirit, from knowing that Jesus Christ is the Son of God to interpreting tongues. The bishop and appointed elders are to discern these gifts. It closes by asking that all be done in Christ’s name, with thanks.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 46–48, “Seek Ye Earnestly the Best Gifts,” invites members to seek spiritual gifts. Which gift in verses 13–25 might you seek, and how would it serve others as verse 26 says?

contextNote.title: Why the gifts are sought
contextNote.text: The Ohio branches had seen spiritual displays that Joseph judged false. Verse 7 names the danger: being “seduced by evil spirits,” or by human commandments. Verse 8 gives the defense: seek the best gifts and remember why they are given. Verse 9 states that reason: they bless those who love God and keep his commandments. They are not given for “a sign” or for selfish use. Verses 11–12 add that no one has every gift, so each gift serves others. Here, to seek a gift means to seek something for the good of the whole church.

passages.title: Keeping the Church’s history became a calling, not a favor
passages.setting: This short revelation came at Kirtland, Ohio, around 8 March 1831. John Whitmer had already served as a scribe for Joseph Smith. He was asked to keep a history, but he said he would rather not. He agreed to serve if the Lord made his will known through Joseph. Joseph then dictated this revelation, and Whitmer accepted. One later copy dates it 7 March.
passages.summary: The revelation names John Whitmer to write and keep a regular history. He is also to help Joseph Smith copy all that is revealed. He may speak in meetings when it is fitting. He is to keep the church record and history continually. The reason given is that Oliver Cowdery has another office. If John is faithful, the Comforter will help him write.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 46–48 draws from this revelation the value of keeping records. According to verse 4, what would help John Whitmer write, and how might that apply to your own record keeping?

contextNote.title: A record kept by assignment
contextNote.text: John Whitmer did not want the job of historian. Verse 1 settles the question by naming him to keep “a regular history.” Verse 3 gives the practical reason: Oliver Cowdery had been appointed to another office. Verse 4 then ties the work to faithfulness and the Comforter’s help. So the history is framed as spiritual work, not only clerical work. In this passage, a “regular” history is a steady, ongoing record kept by calling.

passages.title: Save now, because the place for the city is not yet revealed
passages.setting: This revelation came at Kirtland, Ohio, on 10 March 1831. More than a hundred Church members from New York were expected to arrive soon. Earlier revelations had told them to gather to Ohio. Ohio members, including Bishop Edward Partridge, asked how to prepare for them. John Whitmer also wrote that some believed Ohio itself was the promised New Jerusalem.
passages.summary: The revelation tells the Ohio members to stay where they live for now. Those who own land should share it with the eastern members. Those without land should buy for the present in nearby regions. All should save money and gain what they can in righteousness. That money will later buy land for an inheritance, “even the city.” The place of the city is not yet revealed. Men will be appointed to learn the place, buy the lands, and begin building. Then families will gather under the direction of the presidency and the bishop.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson covering sections 46–48 includes this counsel about receiving the gathering Saints. How do verses 2–4 ask members with land and members without land to prepare in different ways?

contextNote.title: A city not yet located
contextNote.text: Some members thought Ohio was already the gathering place. Verse 5 corrects that idea: “The place is not yet to be revealed.” Verse 1 explains why members should stay put “for the present time.” Verse 4 shows what the waiting is for: saving money to buy land for the city. Verse 6 adds the order of events: appointed men first, then families. In this passage, waiting is an active stage of preparation, not a delay.

passages.title: Shaker beliefs are answered on baptism, marriage, and Christ’s return
passages.setting: This revelation came at Kirtland, Ohio, on 7 May 1831. Leman Copley, a recent convert, had once belonged to the Shakers and kept some of their beliefs. Shakers taught that Christ had already returned in a woman, Ann Lee, and they practiced celibacy. Copley wanted his former community at North Union, near Cleveland, to hear the gospel. Joseph Smith asked the Lord about these questions. Sidney Rigdon read the revelation to the Shakers the next day, and they rejected it.
passages.summary: The revelation sends Sidney Rigdon and Parley P. Pratt to preach to the Shakers. Leman Copley is to go too, teaching only what the other two teach him. It says the Shakers want part of the truth, but not all, and must repent. It restates Peter’s message: believe, repent, be baptized, and receive the Holy Ghost. It says marriage is ordained of God and that meat is given for human use. It warns against wasting flesh and against one person possessing more than another. It says the Son of Man will not come as a woman or as a man traveling the earth. It ends with signs before Christ’s coming and a promise to go before them.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 49–50 uses this revelation to teach truths about marriage and the Savior’s coming. What reasons do verses 15–17 give for why marriage is “ordained of God”?

contextNote.title: Answering a claim about the Second Coming
contextNote.text: The Shakers believed Christ had already returned in Ann Lee. Verse 22 answers that claim directly. The Son of Man will not come “in the form of a woman,” nor as a traveling man. Verse 7 adds that no one knows the hour or day of his coming. Verse 23 tells the hearers what to watch for instead: heavens shaken and the earth reeling. So the revelation treats the coming as public and cosmic, not hidden in one person. In this passage, being “not deceived” means waiting for signs no one could miss.

passages.title: What is of God edifies both the preacher and the hearer
passages.setting: This revelation came at Kirtland, Ohio, on 9 May 1831. Ohio branches had seen fainting, contortions, and claimed visions in their meetings. A local newspaper reported young converts rolling on floors. Joseph Smith had worked to curb these displays since February, but the problems went on. Elders who could not tell true spirits from false asked him for guidance.
passages.summary: The revelation warns the elders that false spirits are deceiving the world. It says there are hypocrites in the Church who will be detected. Then the Lord invites the elders to reason together, face to face. He asks what they were ordained to do, and answers: preach by the Spirit. Teaching and receiving by the Spirit of truth edifies both sides. What does not edify is darkness, and what is of God is light. For a spirit they cannot understand, they are to ask the Father in Jesus’s name. It sends Joseph Wakefield, Parley P. Pratt, and John Corrill to strengthen the churches, and calls Edward Partridge to repent.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 49–50, “That Which Is of God Is Light,” draws on verse 24 about growing light. Using verses 21–23, how could you tell whether a lesson or talk was taught and received by the Spirit?

contextNote.title: Edification as the test
contextNote.text: The elders had accepted spirits they could not understand as coming from God. Verses 17–20 ask two questions: how is truth preached, and how is it received? The answer to both is “by the Spirit of truth.” Verse 22 gives the result: preacher and hearer understand each other and rejoice together. Verse 23 turns that result into a test: what does not edify is not of God. Verse 24 adds that light received leads to more light. In this passage, to edify means to build an understanding that both sides share.

passages.title: Consecration gives each family a secured portion by need
passages.setting: This revelation came at Thompson, Ohio, on 20 May 1831. About sixty members from Colesville, New York, had just arrived under Newel Knight’s lead. They settled on land Leman Copley offered at Thompson. Bishop Edward Partridge was responsible for settling them under the law of consecration. He asked for direction, and Joseph Smith inquired of the Lord. Copley soon withdrew his offer, so the plan was not carried out there.
passages.summary: The revelation gives Edward Partridge directions for organizing the newly arrived people. He and his chosen helpers are to assign each family a portion by its needs. Each person receives a written deed that secures his portion. If a person transgresses and is judged unworthy to belong, he keeps only the deeded portion, not what he consecrated. An agent is to use the remaining money for food and clothing. The bishop is to keep a storehouse for whatever exceeds the people’s needs. The land is consecrated to them “for a little season.” Faithful, just, and wise stewards are promised eternal life.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 51–57, “A Faithful, a Just, and a Wise Steward,” takes its title from verse 19. What does verse 9 ask of each person, and how might you practice it with what you manage?

contextNote.title: Equal does not mean identical
contextNote.text: The Colesville members arrived needing land and support all at once. Verse 3 tells the bishop how to divide what they had. Each family is to be “equal,” but according to its “circumstances,” “wants,” and needs. Verse 4 then secures each portion with a written deed. Verse 9 explains the goal: that the people “may be one.” In this passage, equality means fair provision for each household’s needs, not the same share for all.

passages.title: Elders go to Missouri two by two with a pattern against deception
passages.setting: This revelation came at Kirtland, Ohio, on 6 June 1831. It followed a Church conference held there in early June. At that conference, men were first ordained to the office of high priest. Participants also reported discerning and rebuking false spirits. Joseph Smith dictated the revelation that night and later said it came by vision.
passages.summary: The revelation names Missouri as the site of the next conference. Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon are to travel there soon. If faithful, they will learn where the land of inheritance is. It pairs many other elders and sends them by different routes, preaching on the way. It warns Lyman Wight that Satan desires to sift him. It gives a pattern for knowing which spirits are of God. It sends Joseph Wakefield and Solomon Humphrey east and moves Heman Basset’s office to Simonds Ryder. It tells all elders to remember the poor, needy, sick, and afflicted.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 51–57 points to the pattern in verses 14–19 for avoiding deception. How could you use verses 15–17 to judge whether a message you hear is of God?

contextNote.title: A pattern for judging spirits
contextNote.text: The June conference included spiritual displays that leaders judged false. Verse 14 promises a pattern “that ye may not be deceived.” Verse 15 starts with the one who prays with a contrite spirit. Verse 16 adds the speaker whose language is “meek and edifieth.” Both are accepted only if they “obey mine ordinances.” Verse 18 gives the contrast: one who is overcome and bears no fruit is not of God. In this passage, the pattern joins inner humility, edifying speech, and obedience.

passages.title: Sidney Gilbert is called to leave the world and serve as agent
passages.setting: This revelation came at Kirtland, Ohio, on 8 June 1831. Algernon Sidney Gilbert was a merchant and the business partner of Newel K. Whitney. Two days earlier, a revelation had named elders to go to Missouri, but not Gilbert. He then asked Joseph Smith to inquire about his own role. Gilbert left for Missouri with Joseph and Sidney Rigdon on 18 June.
passages.summary: The revelation tells Sidney Gilbert that his prayers about his calling were heard. The voice speaks as the one crucified for the sins of the world. It commands him to forsake the world. He is to be ordained an elder to preach faith, repentance, and remission of sins. He is also to be an agent for the Church where the bishop appoints. He is to travel with Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon. More will be made known according to his labor, and only those who endure are saved.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 51–57 includes this call to Sidney Gilbert. What do verses 2–4 suggest about bringing ordinary skills, like Gilbert’s business work, into the Lord’s service?

contextNote.title: What forsaking the world asked of a merchant
contextNote.text: Gilbert asked what his calling in the Church should be. Verse 2 answers first with a command: “forsake the world.” Verse 3 then gives a spiritual office, an elder who preaches. Verse 4 gives a practical one: an agent for the Church. So the call did not discard his business skills; it redirected them. Verse 6 calls these only “the first ordinances” he would receive. In this passage, forsaking the world means changing whom one’s work serves.

passages.title: A broken covenant sends the Colesville Saints on to Missouri
passages.setting: This revelation came at Kirtland, Ohio, on 10 June 1831. The Colesville members had settled on Leman Copley’s farm in Thompson, Ohio. After the failed Shaker mission, Copley went back on the arrangement and ordered them off his land. The group was also divided over consecration, and some showed selfishness. Newel Knight, who presided over them, went to Kirtland to ask Joseph Smith what to do.
passages.summary: The revelation speaks to Newel Knight and tells him to stand fast in his office. If his people want to escape their enemies, they must repent and become humble. It says the covenant they made has been broken and is now void. It pronounces woe on the one by whom the offense came. Those who kept the covenant will obtain mercy. The group is told to flee, choose a leader, and travel west to Missouri. There they are to earn a living until a place is prepared. It ends by urging patience in tribulation and promising rest.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 51–57 includes this counsel to the Colesville Saints. What does verse 10 ask of them during their move, and what does it promise?

contextNote.title: When a covenant fails
contextNote.text: The Colesville members had planned to live by consecration on Copley’s land. Verse 4 states the result of the broken agreement: the covenant is “void and of none effect.” Verse 5 places the blame on the one “by whom this offense cometh.” Verse 6 still promises mercy to those who kept the covenant. Verse 7 then turns from blame to action: leave the land and go. In this passage, a void covenant ends the arrangement but not the promise to the faithful.

passages.title: A printer’s skills are called into the Church’s work
passages.setting: William W. Phelps was a newspaper editor and printer from Canandaigua, New York. He bought a Book of Mormon in 1830 and met Joseph Smith that December. In spring 1831 he spent thirty days in jail at Lyons, apparently over a debt. After his release, he moved his family to Ohio. He reached Kirtland by 14 June 1831, and Joseph Smith asked the Lord about him.
passages.summary: The revelation tells William Phelps that he is called and chosen. If baptized with an eye single to God’s glory, he will receive forgiveness and the Holy Spirit. Then Joseph Smith is to ordain him an elder to preach repentance and baptism. He may give the Holy Spirit to those who are contrite. He is to help Oliver Cowdery with printing and with writing books for schools. He is to travel with Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon to the land of inheritance. Joseph Coe is to go with them as well.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 51–57 includes this call to William W. Phelps. According to verse 4, why were schoolbooks to be written, and who were they meant to help?

contextNote.title: Printing and schoolbooks as Church work
contextNote.text: Phelps arrived in Kirtland with years of experience as a printer and editor. Verse 4 puts that experience to use for the Church. He is to help Oliver Cowdery print, and to select and write books for schools. The reason given is that “little children also may receive instruction.” Verse 5 ties this work to a place, the land of inheritance. In this passage, printing belongs to the Church’s teaching mission, reaching even children.

passages.title: The Lord revokes commands when his servants will not act
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 15 June 1831. A revelation nine days earlier had paired Thomas B. Marsh and Ezra Thayre for a mission to Missouri. Marsh was ready to leave, but Thayre was not, so Marsh asked what to do. Thayre had paid money toward the farm where he lived and may have wanted a land title first. Meanwhile the Colesville Saints at Thompson wanted Newel Knight to stay and lead their move west.
passages.summary: The revelation opens with a warning to the rebellious among those who profess the Lord’s name. It says the Lord commands and also revokes as he sees fit. It cancels the mission of Marsh and Thayre and sends Selah J. Griffin with Marsh instead. It also cancels the mission of Griffin and Newel Knight because of rebellion at Thompson. Knight is to stay and lead the contrite there to Missouri. If Thayre repents of pride and selfishness, he may still go to Missouri; if not, he must take back his money and be cut off. If Joseph Smith must repay that money, the Lord promises to repay him in Missouri. The revelation ends with woes on selfish rich and greedy poor, and a blessing on the pure in heart.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 51–57 invites readers to weigh how they use what God gives them. Verses 16–18 judge both rich and poor by the heart: what does each group lack or have?

contextNote.title: Why a command can be withdrawn
contextNote.text: Marsh needed to know whether a broken pairing still bound him. Verse 4 answers that the Lord both commands and revokes as seems good to him. Verse 3 sets the condition: cutting off comes after a command is given and broken. Verses 5–6 then apply the rule twice. Thayre’s delay ends one pairing, and the rebellion at Thompson ends another. Verse 4 places the burden “upon the heads of the rebellious,” not on those who obeyed. In this passage, to revoke means to reassign the work when people fail to act.

passages.title: Independence is named the center place of Zion
passages.setting: Joseph Smith reached Independence, Jackson County, Missouri, on 14 July 1831. A June revelation had sent him and other elders there from Ohio. Oliver Cowdery and other missionaries were already in the area after preaching to American Indians. Joseph Smith later wrote that he pondered those people and asked when and where Zion would be built. He dictated this revelation on 20 July; the original is lost.
passages.summary: The revelation tells the elders gathered in Missouri that this land is appointed for the gathering of the Saints. It calls it the land of promise and the place for the city of Zion. Independence is the center place, and a temple lot lies west of the courthouse. The Saints are to buy land there and westward to the line “between Jew and Gentile,” as far as they can. Sidney Gilbert is to act as agent, buy land, and open a store. Edward Partridge is to divide inheritances to the Saints. William W. Phelps is to be printer, with Oliver Cowdery helping to copy and correct. These men are to settle in Zion, and the bishop and agent are to prepare for arriving families.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 51–57 treats the work in Zion as stewardship. In verses 6–13, what task does each named man receive, and how does each serve the gathering?

contextNote.title: A place on the map at last
contextNote.text: For months the city of Zion had no known location. An 1830 revelation had placed it only on the borders by the Lamanites (D&C 28:9). Verse 3 answers with a town and a lot: Independence, west of the courthouse. Verse 4 turns that answer into a task, telling the Saints to buy the land. Verses 6–8 then assign people to handle money, land, and goods. In this passage, “center place” names a real site to be purchased and settled.

passages.title: Do good of your own free will, not only when commanded
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Jackson County on 1 August 1831, probably at Independence. Elders arriving in July found fewer than ten converts and a rough frontier town. Bishop Edward Partridge had disagreed with Joseph Smith over the quality of land being bought. That week Colesville Saints from Thompson, Ohio, also arrived. Many wanted to know the Lord’s will for them in the new gathering place.
passages.summary: The revelation tells the elders that blessings come after much tribulation. It says they were sent to obey, to lay Zion’s foundation, and to prepare a feast for the poor. Edward Partridge is to judge in Israel and divide inheritances, but he must repent of unbelief. The Saints must keep the laws of the land. The Lord will not command in all things, so people should do much good of their own free will. Martin Harris is to lay his money before the bishop, and he and Phelps must repent. Sidney Rigdon is to describe Zion in writing and dedicate the land and temple site. Joseph Smith, Rigdon, and Cowdery are to return home, Ziba Peterson loses his office, and others preach on the way.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 58–59 draws out the call to act without waiting to be told. Verses 3–4 ask the Saints to wait for blessings, while verse 27 asks them to act now. What good cause could you begin this week without being asked?

contextNote.title: Agents unto themselves
contextNote.text: The Saints in Missouri wanted detailed direction for a hard new place. Verse 26 answers that the Lord does not mean to command in all things. A servant who must be compelled in everything is called slothful. Verse 27 asks instead for people “anxiously engaged in a good cause” by free will. Verse 28 gives the reason: the power is in them, and they are agents unto themselves. Verse 29 draws the contrast with one who waits for orders and obeys with doubt. In this passage, being an agent means acting on one’s own to do good.

passages.title: Zion’s Saints are to keep the Sabbath with thanks
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Jackson County, Missouri, on 7 August 1831. In the days before, the land had been dedicated for Zion and a temple site dedicated. That morning Polly Knight, wife of Joseph Knight Sr., died, the first Church member to die there. Sunday worship was lax among local settlers, and earlier Church laws said little about the Sabbath. Joseph Smith had been told to return to Ohio, so the Saints needed written guidance.
passages.summary: The revelation blesses those who came to Zion with an eye single to God’s glory. Those who live will inherit the earth, and those who die will rest and receive a crown. It then gives commandments to love God and neighbor and not to steal, commit adultery, or kill. It asks for thanks in all things and the sacrifice of a broken heart and contrite spirit. The Saints are to go to the house of prayer and offer their sacraments on the Lord’s day. That day they are to rest, confess their sins, and prepare food with singleness of heart. If they do these things with thanks and glad hearts, the fulness of the earth is theirs. God is offended only by those who do not confess his hand in all things and do not obey.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 58–59 connects Sabbath worship and gratitude. Verses 9–14 list what the Saints should do on the Lord’s day; which of those actions could you add to your next Sabbath?

contextNote.title: A day to stay unspotted
contextNote.text: The Saints were building Zion among settlers who largely ignored Sunday worship. Verse 9 gives the reason for the Sabbath command: to keep oneself “unspotted from the world” more fully. The means is going to the house of prayer and offering sacraments on the holy day. Verse 10 adds that the day is set apart to rest from labor and to worship. Verses 13–14 then describe fasting as “rejoicing and prayer” with a glad heart. In this passage, keeping the Sabbath is a weekly practice that sets the Saints apart from their surroundings.

passages.title: Elders who hide their talent through fear will lose it
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Independence, Missouri, on 8 August 1831. The elders there had helped dedicate the land for Zion and the temple site. With that work done, many were anxious to go home. A later Joseph Smith history says they asked him what they should do. This revelation was his answer.
passages.summary: The revelation tells the elders who are to return that the Lord is pleased they came. But some would not open their mouths and hid their talent for fear of man. If they are not more faithful, even what they have will be taken. The elders are to make or buy a boat and travel quickly toward Saint Louis. From there Sidney Rigdon, Joseph Smith, and Oliver Cowdery go to Cincinnati to preach. The rest go two by two and preach on the way home, not in haste. Edward Partridge is to give them money, to be repaid by those able. Elders still coming to Zion must not bury their talent and must shake off dust only in secret.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 60–63 teaches that the Lord stays with those who share the gospel. Verse 2 names “the fear of man” as the reason some kept silent; what does verse 7 promise those who speak?

contextNote.title: A talent kept quiet
contextNote.text: The elders had finished their work in Zion and asked what to do next. Before giving travel plans, verse 2 names a problem among them. Because of “the fear of man,” some would “not open their mouths” to preach. Verse 3 states the result: if they stay unfaithful, what they have will be taken. Verse 13 repeats the charge for elders still on the road: do not bury your talent. In this passage, the talent is the gift and charge to preach, and hiding it means staying silent.

passages.title: Danger on the river brings both a promise and a new route
passages.setting: Joseph Smith and about ten elders left Independence by canoe on the Missouri River in August 1831. On the third day they met dangers on the river and camped at McIlwaine’s Bend. Joseph Smith’s history says William W. Phelps saw the destroyer riding on the waters in vision. JSP editors note that this detail likely came from Phelps himself. Joseph Smith dictated this revelation on the riverbank on 12 August 1831.
passages.summary: The revelation forgives the assembled elders who confess their sins with humble hearts. It says the whole company need not speed down the river while people on either side perish in unbelief. It says the Lord has decreed many destructions on these waters, but the faithful will not perish. Sidney Gilbert and William Phelps are to hurry ahead on their mission. It says the Lord blessed the waters in the beginning and cursed them in the last days through John. Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Oliver Cowdery are to travel only by canal, and Saints bound for Zion are to go by land. The three are not to preach to the wicked until they reach Cincinnati. Reynolds Cahoon and Samuel Smith are to stay together, and the revelation closes with “be of good cheer” and a call to watch and pray.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 60–63 stresses the Lord’s presence with His servants. Verse 36 says “be of good cheer” right after warnings of danger; how do verses 6 and 36–37 together describe that presence?

contextNote.title: Faith and caution on the water
contextNote.text: The elders had just met real danger on the Missouri River. Verse 5 says the Lord has decreed many destructions upon these waters. Verse 6 answers the fear that follows: “all flesh is in mine hand.” The faithful among them, it says, will not perish by the waters. Yet verses 23–24 still set a safer route, by canal and then by land. In this passage, the promise of verse 6 stands beside practical caution about how to travel.

passages.title: Testimony already borne is recorded in heaven
passages.setting: Joseph Smith and his companions were traveling home from Independence to Ohio in August 1831. On 13 August they crossed the Missouri River at Chariton, Missouri. There they met Hyrum Smith, John Murdock, David Whitmer, and Harvey Whitlock, still headed to Zion. Murdock had been ill, and he and Hyrum had stayed in Chariton while he recovered. After a joyful meeting, Joseph Smith dictated this revelation on the riverbank.
passages.summary: The voice in verse 1 speaks as Jesus Christ, the elders’ advocate who knows human weakness. It tells the elders who have not reached Zion that their mission is not yet full. Their testimony is recorded in heaven, angels rejoice over them, and their sins are forgiven. They are to continue to Zion, hold a meeting, rejoice, and offer a sacrament. Afterward they may return together or two by two, as long as they are faithful. Those who wish may ride horses, mules, or carriages if they receive this with thanks. These matters are left to their judgment and the Spirit. The revelation ends: “I am with the faithful always.”

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 60–63 draws its title from verse 9. Which choices in verses 5–8 does the Lord leave to the elders’ judgment, and what condition does verse 7 attach?

contextNote.title: Credit before arrival
contextNote.text: These elders had preached their way west and had not yet reached Zion. Verse 2 says their mission is not yet full. Verse 3 explains why they are blessed anyway: their testimony is “recorded in heaven.” Angels look on it and rejoice, and their sins are forgiven. Verse 6 adds the purpose of the meeting: the faithful are brought together to rejoice in Missouri. In this passage, the heavenly record means their preaching already counts before the journey ends.

passages.title: Zion must be bought, gathered slowly, and spoken of with care
passages.setting: Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Oliver Cowdery reached Kirtland from Missouri on 27 August 1831. They found that many members had left the Church while they were away. Joseph Smith later called the land of Zion the most important temporal concern of the time. He asked the Lord about gathering the Saints and buying land. He dictated this revelation on 30 August, probably at the Isaac Morley farm. Cowdery wrote the earliest surviving copy.
passages.summary: The revelation opens with a warning to the wicked and rebellious. It says signs follow faith rather than create it, and it rebukes sign seekers and adulterers. The Saints are to gather to Zion, but not in haste. Zion can be gained only by purchase or by blood, and they are forbidden to shed blood. So Titus Billings is to sell the farm, and Newel K. Whitney and Oliver Cowdery are to raise money. The revelation describes the resurrection and the separation of the wicked at Christ’s coming. It rejects Sidney Rigdon’s written description of Zion and tells him to write another. It warns against using the Lord’s name without authority.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 60–63 teaches that signs follow faith. Verse 64 says sacred things must be spoken “with care, and by constraint of the Spirit” through prayer. How might that verse shape the way you share a spiritual experience?

contextNote.title: Signs follow faith
contextNote.text: The revelation addresses people among the Saints who wanted signs. Verse 9 reverses their order: faith does not come by signs, but signs follow believers. Verse 10 adds that signs come by God’s will, not as people please. Verse 7 says sign seekers will see signs, “but not unto salvation,” as verse 11 explains. Verse 12 names the fault as seeking signs for faith rather than for the good of others. In this passage, a sign is a result of faith used to bless people, not a proof that produces belief.

passages.title: The Lord forgives whom he will, but his people must forgive all
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 11 September 1831. He was preparing to move to Hiram to resume his Bible revision. Some who went to Missouri that summer came back disappointed. Ezra Booth had turned against Joseph Smith, and on 6 September a conference barred Booth from preaching. Edward Partridge had also clashed with Joseph Smith in Missouri over the land being bought.
passages.summary: The revelation tells the elders that the Lord has forgiven their sins this once. Joseph Smith keeps the keys of the mysteries while he obeys, though he too has sinned. The elders must forgive all men, while the Lord forgives whom he will. Ezra Booth and Isaac Morley are named for not keeping the law, and Morley is forgiven. Edward Partridge has sinned and will be forgiven if he repents. Kirtland is to remain a strong hold for five years, so Frederick G. Williams keeps his farm. The revelation calls today a day of sacrifice and tithing, and says great things come from small things. It ends by saying the Lord requires the heart and a willing mind, and that Zion will flourish.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 64–66 takes its title from verse 34. Verse 11 offers words to say in your heart toward someone who wronged you; how do verses 9–10 explain why that matters?

contextNote.title: Leaving judgment to God
contextNote.text: Leaders had quarreled in Missouri, and Ezra Booth had turned against Joseph Smith. Verse 8 recalls disciples of old who would not forgive each other and were chastened. Verse 9 says the one who does not forgive carries “the greater sin” before the Lord. Verse 10 sets the rule: the Lord forgives whom he will, but they must forgive all. Verses 12–13 add that church discipline still applies to the unrepentant, without withholding forgiveness. In this passage, forgiving means leaving judgment to God, as verse 11 phrases it.

passages.title: Prayer asks for God’s kingdom to fill the earth
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Hiram, Ohio, on 30 October 1831. It may have come during a Sunday meeting at the home of John and Elsa Johnson. William E. McLellin, who preached there that day, made an early copy. He linked it to the request “Thy kingdom come” in the Lord’s Prayer. The scribe of the original is unknown.
passages.summary: The revelation describes a mighty voice from on high calling people to “prepare ye the way of the Lord” and make his paths straight. It says the keys of the kingdom of God are committed to men on earth. From there the gospel will roll forth like the stone cut from the mountain without hands. The voice calls people to prepare the supper of the Lamb and make ready for the Bridegroom. It tells them to pray and make known the Lord’s works. They are to call on the Lord so his kingdom may go forth. It says the Son of Man will come down to meet the kingdom of God set up on earth. The section ends as a prayer that the kingdom of God go forth so the kingdom of heaven may come.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 64–66 presents this section as a revelation on prayer. Verses 5–6 pray for two kingdoms; how could their relationship shape what you mean when you pray “thy kingdom come”?

contextNote.title: Keys already on the earth
contextNote.text: The revelation asks how God’s kingdom will reach the whole earth. Verse 2 answers that the keys are already “committed unto man on the earth” in this day. It compares the gospel to the stone in Daniel, cut out without hands, that fills the earth. Verses 4–5 then turn the hearer to prayer for that kingdom to go forth. Verse 6 links the two kingdoms: one goes forth so that the other may come. In this passage, the keys are authority already on earth, and prayer asks God to spread it.

passages.title: A new convert is clean, but not all, and must keep repenting
passages.setting: William E. McLellin, a recent convert from Paris, Illinois, met Joseph Smith at a conference in Orange, Ohio, on 25–26 October 1831. He then traveled with Joseph to Hiram, arriving on 29 October. McLellin had privately asked the Lord five questions, which he never recorded. At his request, Joseph Smith dictated this revelation that day, probably in the John Johnson home. McLellin wrote it down and said it answered his questions fully.
passages.summary: The voice in verse 1 speaks as the Redeemer to William McLellin and blesses him for turning from his sins and receiving the everlasting covenant. It says he is clean, “but not all,” and must repent of what the Lord will show him. He is to preach from land to land where the gospel has not been heard. He is not to go to Zion yet, but to the eastern lands with Samuel Smith. He is to lay hands on the sick, be patient in affliction, and not be cumbered. It warns him against adultery, a temptation that has troubled him. If he continues to the end, he will receive a crown of eternal life.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 64–66 sees in this revelation the Lord’s personal care for one man. Verse 3 calls McLellin “clean, but not all”; which instructions in verses 9–12 would help him finish that work?

contextNote.title: Clean, but not all
contextNote.text: McLellin had silently asked questions he never wrote down. JSP editors think one concern was his standing before God. Verse 1 blesses him for turning away from his sins. Verse 3 then limits the blessing: he is clean, “but not all.” The same verse promises the Lord will show him what still needs repenting. Verse 10 names one such matter, a temptation to adultery. In this passage, being clean is real but partial, and the remedy is ongoing repentance.

passages.title: Elders must match the revelations or testify that they are true
passages.setting: Elders met in conference at Hiram, Ohio, on 1–2 November 1831. They voted to publish Joseph Smith’s revelations as the Book of Commandments. Several elders signed a statement that the revelations came by inspiration. Some held back, partly over doubts about the plain language Joseph used. Joseph dictated this revelation during the conference, but the exact day is uncertain. His later history says William McLellin then tried to write a revelation and failed.
passages.summary: The revelation speaks to the assembled elders and says their prayers have been heard. It says fears in their hearts kept them from a blessing they sought. It notes they have watched Joseph Smith’s language and imperfections. It then sets a test: pick the least revelation and let the wisest elder write one like it. If they can, they may say they do not know the revelations are true. If they cannot, they are condemned unless they testify. It closes with a promise that the humble will one day see God by the Spirit.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 67–70 invites readers to value the revelations and seek their own witness. What do verses 3 and 10 say kept the elders from that witness, and what were they asked to set aside?

contextNote.title: A test aimed at doubts about language
contextNote.text: Some elders doubted the revelations because Joseph Smith’s wording seemed plain. Verse 5 names that doubt directly: they knew his language and his imperfections. Verse 6 answers with a test, not an argument. Verse 7 lets them withhold their witness if they can write one “like unto” the least revelation. Verse 8 gives the other result: if they fail, they must “bear record” or stand condemned. Verse 3 had said fears blocked them, which ties the doubt to their own hearts. In this passage, the test measures whether the revelations came “from above,” as verse 9 says, not how polished they are.

passages.title: Words spoken by the Holy Ghost are scripture
passages.setting: This revelation is dated 1 November 1831, at Hiram, Ohio, during the conference on publishing the revelations. Orson Hyde, Luke Johnson, Lyman Johnson, and William McLellin asked Joseph Smith to learn the Lord’s will for them. The first part answers them, and the rest speaks to the whole church. It may first have been two revelations later copied together. In 1835 Joseph Smith expanded the text for the Doctrine and Covenants. The added passages concern who may serve as bishop and how bishops are appointed.
passages.summary: The revelation begins with Orson Hyde’s call to preach by the Spirit. It makes his call a pattern for all who are ordained to go forth. Whatever they speak when moved by the Holy Ghost will be scripture. It sends Hyde, Luke Johnson, Lyman Johnson, and William McLellin into all the world to preach and baptize. It then gives rules for bishops, including the rights of literal descendants of Aaron. Parents in Zion must teach their children faith, repentance, baptism, and the Holy Ghost by age eight. The Lord says he is displeased with idlers and greed in Zion. Oliver Cowdery is to carry these sayings there.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 67–70 draws on this revelation’s teaching about speaking by the Holy Ghost and teaching children. What do verses 25–28 ask parents in Zion to teach, and by what age?

contextNote.title: What makes spoken words scripture
contextNote.text: The four men had asked what the Lord wanted of them. Verse 3 gives a standard, not a script: speak “as they are moved upon by the Holy Ghost” wherever they go. Verse 4 says such speech is scripture, and the will, mind, word, and voice of the Lord. Verse 2 widens this from Orson Hyde to all who are sent out. Verse 6 gives the reason they need not fear: the Lord will “stand by” them. In this passage, scripture is defined by its source in the Holy Ghost, not by a printed book.

passages.title: Revelations and records must reach Zion with a faithful companion
passages.setting: Oliver Cowdery was assigned to carry the compiled revelations to Independence, Missouri, for printing. He was also to take money donated for the church there. On 11 November 1831, at Hiram, Ohio, Joseph Smith dictated this revelation. It sent John Whitmer, the church historian, with him. The two left for Missouri on 20 November. The Joseph Smith Papers editors call the date probable but not certain.
passages.summary: The revelation says Oliver Cowdery should not travel alone with the commandments and the money. It names John Whitmer to go with him. Whitmer is to keep writing a history of important things about the church. He is to take counsel from Cowdery and others. Elders abroad are to send accounts of their stewardships to Zion. Zion is to be the place that receives these things. Whitmer is also to travel among the churches to gather knowledge and records. The work is for the generations who will grow up in Zion.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 67–70 uses verse 1 to teach that “true and faithful” friends help us follow Jesus Christ. According to verses 3 and 8, what was John Whitmer, Oliver’s faithful companion, to record, and for whom?

contextNote.title: A historian sent with the revelations
contextNote.text: The revelation first deals with safety: precious papers and money needed a trustworthy second traveler. Verse 2 chooses John Whitmer for that task. Verse 3 adds a lasting duty, to keep “writing and making a history” of the church. Verses 7–8 explain how he would gather it, by traveling and copying from church to church. Verse 8 also gives the purpose: the record is for “the rising generations” in Zion. In this passage, history means a gathered record meant to serve people not yet born.

passages.title: Stewards over the revelations must share their gains with Zion
passages.setting: A series of conferences at Hiram, Ohio, ended on 12 November 1831. The last one voted that the revelations were worth the riches of the whole earth to the church. Joseph Smith asked the elders to support those who had worked on the church’s sacred writings. He dictated this revelation that day, possibly in answer to a question. The exact question is not recorded.
passages.summary: The revelation speaks to Zion and to church members far away. It appoints six men as stewards over the revelations: Joseph Smith, Martin Harris, Oliver Cowdery, John Whitmer, Sidney Rigdon, and William W. Phelps. They will give an account of this stewardship at judgment. They are to manage the revelations and their benefits, not give them away. What exceeds their needs goes to the Lord’s storehouse for Zion. No one is exempt from this law, not even the bishop. Stewards over spiritual things deserve support, and all must be equal in temporal things.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 67–70 takes its title from the conference vote behind this revelation. How do verses 7–8 and 14 describe what the stewards owed to Zion?

contextNote.title: Equality as the condition for the Spirit
contextNote.text: The stewards would earn money from publishing, which raised the question of who should benefit. Verse 7 sends whatever exceeds their needs to the Lord’s storehouse. Verse 10 says no member is exempt, and verse 11 names the bishop and the storehouse agent. Verse 14 then sets the rule that “you shall be equal” in temporal things. It adds a warning that grudging equality would cause the Spirit to be withheld. Verse 13 shows what is at stake: abundance is multiplied “through the manifestations of the Spirit” to those who serve. In this passage, equality is a shared willingness to give, tied directly to spiritual gifts.

passages.title: Answer critics openly, for their weapons will not prosper
passages.setting: Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon were revising the Bible at the John Johnson home in Hiram, Ohio. Ezra Booth, a former member, had published critical letters in the Ohio Star of Ravenna since October 1831. Symonds Rider, also disaffected, had given a February 1831 revelation to another local paper. On 1 December 1831, Joseph dictated this revelation, which set the Bible work aside so both men could preach. Rigdon later challenged both critics to public meetings, and both declined.
passages.summary: The revelation tells Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon that the time has come to preach. They are to expound the scriptures by the Spirit given them. They are to preach in the nearby regions and in the church for a season. This work will prepare the way for revelations still to come. They are to invite their enemies to meet them in public and in private. If they are faithful, their critics’ shame will be shown. The revelation promises that no weapon formed against them will prosper. It closes by telling them to keep the commandments.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 71–75 takes its title, “No Weapon That Is Formed against You Shall Prosper,” from verse 9. According to verses 4 and 7, what were Joseph and Sidney to do instead of staying silent?

contextNote.title: A promise given with an assignment
contextNote.text: Critics were attacking the church in nearby newspapers. Verse 7 tells Joseph and Sidney to answer by calling their enemies to meet them openly. Verse 8 even invites the critics to bring their “strong reasons” against the Lord. Verse 9 gives the ground for this confidence: no weapon formed against them will prosper. Verse 10 adds that opponents will be confounded “in mine own due time,” not at once. Here the promise does not remove opposition; it backs an open, faithful reply to it.

passages.title: A second bishop must account for stewards and certify Saints for Zion
passages.setting: Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon traveled from Hiram to Kirtland, Ohio, on 3 December 1831. The next day high priests and members met there to learn their duties. Joseph dictated three revelations that day, later printed together as this section. The first called the Kirtland merchant Newel K. Whitney as bishop in Ohio, while Edward Partridge served as bishop in Missouri. The other two set Whitney’s duties and rules for moving to Zion.
passages.summary: The first revelation tells the high priests at Kirtland that a bishop is needed in this region. Elders here must account for their stewardship to him, with records sent to the bishop in Zion. It names Newel K. Whitney as that bishop. The second revelation sets his duties: keep the storehouse, receive funds, and supply the elders. Debts elders cannot pay go to the bishop in Zion, and their spiritual labors answer for them. Elders need this bishop’s certificate to be accepted in Zion, and publishing stewards may claim his help. The third requires members moving to Zion to carry a certificate from three elders or a bishop.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 71–75 includes this revelation’s teaching on stewardship. According to verses 3–5, to whom did the Kirtland elders give an account, and what did faithfulness prepare them for?

contextNote.title: Accounting as the mark of a steward
contextNote.text: The Ohio church had grown, but its bishop, Edward Partridge, now lived in Missouri. Verse 2 supplies a local bishop for “this part of the Lord’s vineyard” in Ohio. Verse 3 explains why the conference acted wisely: every steward must give an account. Verse 4 links that account to a reward in the mansions of the Father. Verses 17–18 show the practical result, a certificate that makes a person acceptable in Zion. In this passage, a steward is someone who holds goods or work for the Lord and reports on it.

passages.title: Preach until conference, then finish the Bible translation
passages.setting: Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon had preached around Hiram and Kirtland, Ohio, since early December 1831. A later history says their preaching calmed feelings stirred by Ezra Booth’s published letters. They returned to Hiram about 8 January 1832. On 10 January, Joseph dictated this revelation in the John Johnson home, probably with Rigdon as scribe. A general conference was due about two weeks later.
passages.summary: The revelation says the elders should keep preaching in the nearby regions until the conference. At the conference their separate missions will be made known. It then tells Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon to translate again. They should also preach nearby until the conference when it is practical. After that they are to continue translating until the work is finished. This plan is a pattern for the elders until more is revealed. It ends by telling them to gird up their loins and be sober.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 71–75 covers this short revelation about balancing duties. How do verses 3–4 divide Joseph and Sidney’s time before and after the conference?

contextNote.title: Balancing two assignments
contextNote.text: Joseph and Sidney had laid the Bible revision aside to answer critics. Verse 3 now says it is “expedient to translate again.” Verse 4 keeps preaching in place “inasmuch as it is practicable” until the conference. After the conference, the same verse says translation should continue “until it be finished” as the main task. Verse 2 explains the pause: the conference would assign the elders their missions. In this passage, “expedient” means what fits the present need, and the need had changed.

passages.title: Little children are holy through Christ, not through the law
passages.setting: John Whitmer copied this explanation of scripture into Revelation Book 1 and dated it only 1830. He gave the place as Wayne County, New York, so it predates Joseph Smith’s move to Ohio in January 1831. Later histories wrongly placed it in January 1832. It explains 1 Corinthians 7:14, a verse often used to support infant baptism. The official heading ties it to questions about baptism, but the exact occasion is not recorded.
passages.summary: The explanation opens by quoting Paul: an unbelieving spouse is sanctified by the believing one. It says that in the apostles’ day unbelieving Jews still kept the law of circumcision. Contention arose when unbelieving husbands wanted their children circumcised under the law of Moses. Those children followed their fathers’ traditions and did not believe the gospel. So Paul wrote, on his own authority, that believers should not marry unbelievers. His aim was to end the tradition that little children are unholy. It concludes that little children are holy, sanctified through the atonement of Jesus Christ.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 71–75 includes this explanation of a passage from Paul. How does verse 7 compare with Moroni 8 in the Book of Mormon on the state of little children?

contextNote.title: Why Paul’s counsel was about children
contextNote.text: Some readers used Paul’s words about unbelieving spouses to argue that infants need baptism. This text reads the passage against a dispute over circumcision instead. Verse 3 names the problem: unbelieving fathers wanted their children placed under the law of Moses. Verse 4 gives the result: those children grew up rejecting the gospel. Verse 6 states Paul’s aim, to end the idea that little children are unholy. Verse 7 then answers that children are “sanctified through the atonement of Jesus Christ” and so are holy. In this passage, “holy” describes children’s standing before God apart from any rite.

passages.title: Missionaries are paired and sent, and their families must be supported
passages.setting: A general conference met at Amherst, Ohio, on 25 January 1832, about fifty miles west of Kirtland. William McLellin later said seventy to eighty church officers attended. Joseph Smith was ordained President of the High Priesthood there. Elders who had offered to preach asked to know the Lord’s will for them. Joseph dictated two revelations that day, now verses 1–22 and 23–36. The 1835 Doctrine and Covenants combined them into one section.
passages.summary: The first revelation tells those who volunteered to preach to go without delay and labor with their might. Faithful workers are promised sheaves, honor, and eternal life. William McLellin’s eastern mission is revoked; he is chastened for murmuring, forgiven, and sent south with Luke Johnson. Orson Hyde, Samuel Smith, Lyman Johnson, and Orson Pratt go east, and other pairs go west and south. Houses that reject them are to be left with the dust shaken off as a testimony. The second revelation asks the church to support the families of those sent out. A man who must provide for his own family may stay and keep his crown, but idlers have no place. It ends by pairing fourteen more men, including Hyrum Smith, Reynolds Cahoon, and Ezra Thayre.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 71–75 includes these mission calls and their care for families. What do verses 24–28 ask of the church, of the missionaries, and of fathers who stay home?

contextNote.title: Two duties that need not compete
contextNote.text: Many elders who volunteered had families who depended on them. Verse 24 makes the support of those families a duty of the church. Verse 25 asks the elders to find places for their families where members are willing. Verse 26 then says those with such support must not fail to go. Verse 28 says the man who must provide for his family “shall in nowise lose his crown” by staying. Verse 29 marks the limit, since the idler has no place in the church. In this passage, providing for a family counts as faithful labor, not as a lesser calling.

passages.title: Through Christ nearly all inherit one of three kingdoms of glory
passages.setting: Joseph Smith returned from the Amherst conference and resumed revising the Bible at the John Johnson home in Hiram, Ohio. Sidney Rigdon was his scribe. Joseph had reasoned that heaven must hold more than one kingdom if people are judged by their deeds. On 16 February 1832, while pondering John 5:29, the two reported seeing a vision together. Philo Dibble later said about twelve men were in the room, but his accounts vary. The vision was printed in The Evening and the Morning Star in July 1832.
passages.summary: The text opens with praise and a promise to reveal mysteries to the faithful. Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon then testify that they saw the Son at the Father’s right hand. They report the fall of Lucifer and the fate of the sons of perdition, who alone are not redeemed. The vision describes the celestial glory, like the sun, for those who receive Christ’s testimony, are baptized, and overcome by faith. The terrestrial glory, like the moon, is for the honorable who were not valiant in that testimony. The telestial glory, like the stars, is for those who did not receive the gospel but did not deny the Holy Spirit. Its inhabitants are numberless, and all will bow to Christ. The writers say they saw more than they were allowed to write.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for section 76 takes its title from verse 6 and centers on the vision’s witness of Christ. Comparing verses 51–53, 74–79, and 82–83, what separates each glory from the next?

contextNote.title: The witness that comes before the kingdoms
contextNote.text: The vision began with a question about the resurrection in John 5:29. Before describing any kingdom, verses 20–23 record what the two men say they saw first: the Son at the Father’s right hand. Verse 22 states their testimony, given “last of all” after many others, that Christ lives. Verse 23 gives the basis: “we saw him” and heard a voice name him the Only Begotten. Verse 24 extends his role to the creation of worlds and their inhabitants. Verses 39–43 later make him the one through whom all but the sons of perdition are saved. In this passage, “testimony” means an eyewitness claim, and the rest of the vision builds on it.

passages.title: John’s symbols in Revelation are explained as beings and eras
passages.setting: Joseph Smith was revising the New Testament in early 1832 and reached the book of Revelation. He was living at Hiram, Ohio, in the home of John and Elsa Johnson. His later history says he received an explanation of John’s Revelation about the start of March. The Joseph Smith Papers date the document to between about 4 and 20 March 1832. Sidney Rigdon or Jesse Gause probably wrote it down.
passages.summary: The section is a list of fifteen questions and answers about Revelation chapters 4 to 11. It says the sea of glass is the earth in its sanctified, eternal state. It says the four beasts were four individual beasts shown to John, representing classes of beings in their glory. Their eyes stand for knowledge and their wings for power. The book with seven seals holds God’s works for the earth’s seven thousand years, one seal for each thousand. The angel from the east and the little book John ate are both tied to Elias, who gathers Israel and restores all things. The trumpets prepare the way for Christ’s coming at the start of the seventh thousand years. The two witnesses are two prophets sent to the Jews after they rebuild Jerusalem.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 77–80, “I Will Lead You Along,” presents this section as a key for reading John’s Revelation. How does verse 2, on spirit in “the likeness” of the body, change how you picture the four beasts?

contextNote.title: A sealed book read as history
contextNote.text: Revelation 5 describes a book sealed with seven seals, and readers had long asked what it held. Verse 6 answers that it holds God’s will, mysteries, and works for this earth. It covers the seven thousand years of the earth’s temporal existence. Verse 7 then assigns each seal to one thousand years. This turns John’s vision into a timeline that the later answers use. Verses 10 and 13 place events at the sixth and seventh seals. Here a “seal” marks a span of time, not only a hidden secret.

passages.title: Equality in earthly things prepares Saints for heavenly things
passages.setting: Joseph Smith came to Kirtland, Ohio, from his home in Hiram on 1 March 1832. He met with high priests about the Church’s publishing and store businesses and dictated this revelation there. Sidney Gilbert had opened a store in Independence, partly funded by Newel K. Whitney of Kirtland. It led to the United Firm, organized in April 1832 and dissolved in 1834. Later editions replaced “firm” and the business terms with “order” and the storehouse for the poor.
passages.summary: The revelation tells high priests in council that the time has come to organize the storehouse for the poor in Kirtland and Zion. It states that if they are not equal in earthly things, they cannot be equal in obtaining heavenly things. It names Newel K. Whitney, Joseph Smith, and Sidney Rigdon to sit in council with the Saints in Zion. It commands them to bind themselves by an everlasting covenant, and whoever breaks it loses office and standing. It names Michael as prince, holding keys under the Holy One. It calls them little children who cannot bear all things yet. Still, it promises to lead them along. It closes by promising that the faithful and wise steward will inherit all things.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 77–80, “I Will Lead You Along,” takes its title from verse 18. According to verses 5–7, how does organizing to care for the poor prepare people for heavenly things?

contextNote.title: Why stores and printing became a covenant
contextNote.text: The council needed a reason to tie stores and printing to a religious covenant. Verse 6 gives it: unequal earthly things block equality in heavenly things. Verse 5 states the goal as being “equal in the bonds” of both. Verse 3 names the means, a storehouse for the poor in Kirtland and Zion. Verse 7 adds that a place in the celestial world requires preparation now. In this passage, being “equal” is a condition of the order, built through shared resources for the poor.

passages.title: Jared Carter is sent east again with the Comforter as guide
passages.setting: Jared Carter had spent late 1831 and early 1832 preaching in Ohio, Pennsylvania, New York, and Vermont. A few weeks after returning home to Amherst, Ohio, he went to Hiram. There he asked Joseph Smith what the Lord wanted for his next season of preaching. Joseph dictated this revelation on 12 March 1832. Carter left on the new mission on 15 April 1832.
passages.summary: The revelation tells Jared Carter to go again into the eastern countries. He is to preach from city to city by the authority of his ordination. It promises to send the Comforter to teach him the truth and where to go. If he is faithful, he will be crowned “again with sheaves.” It tells him to let his heart be glad and not to fear. The speaker names himself as Jesus Christ.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 77–80, “I Will Lead You Along,” shows the Lord guiding servants like Jared Carter. What does verse 2 promise Jared Carter about the choices the revelation itself leaves open?

contextNote.title: A guide for a route not yet chosen
contextNote.text: Carter came to Hiram asking where and how to preach next. Verse 1 sets only the region: the “eastern countries,” from place to place. Verse 2 leaves the details to the Comforter, who will teach him the way he should go. Verse 3 looks back on his earlier mission with the word “again.” Sheaves are bundles of harvested grain, an image of converts gathered in. In this passage, the Comforter is a guide for the journey as well as a teacher of truth.

passages.title: Where to preach matters less than what one knows
passages.setting: Stephen Burnett was a young Ohio convert, ordained a high priest at seventeen in October 1831. A January 1832 revelation paired him with Ruggles Eames, but it is unclear whether they served. On 7 March 1832, at Hiram, Ohio, Joseph Smith dictated this new call. Eden Smith fell ill that same day, so the two did not preach together until August 1832. One manuscript copy dates it 17 March, but editors favor 7 March.
passages.summary: The revelation tells Stephen Burnett to go into the world and preach to all who hear his voice. Because he wants a companion, it gives him Eden Smith. It says they “cannot go amiss” whether they go north, south, east, or west. It tells them to declare what they have heard, believe, and know to be true. It closes by naming the one who calls them as Jesus Christ.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 77–80, “I Will Lead You Along,” includes this short call to two missionaries. What have you heard, believed, and come to know that verse 4 would invite you to declare?

contextNote.title: Preaching from what one knows
contextNote.text: A new missionary might worry most about where to go. Verse 3 sets that worry aside: any direction will do. Verse 4 moves the weight to the message itself. They must declare what they have heard, believe, and know to be true. The three verbs move from hearing to belief to knowledge. In this passage, the call rests on personal witness, not on a chosen route.

passages.title: A counselor in the Presidency serves by strengthening the weak
passages.setting: Joseph Smith had been ordained President of the High Priesthood at Amherst, Ohio, in January 1832. On 8 March he chose Jesse Gause and Sidney Rigdon as counselors. This revelation, dated 15 March 1832 at Hiram, was first addressed to Gause. Gause did not continue faithfully and was excommunicated in December 1832. Frederick G. Williams’s name later replaced his, and Williams was ordained a counselor on 18 March 1833.
passages.summary: The revelation calls Frederick G. Williams to be a high priest and a counselor to Joseph Smith. It says Joseph holds the keys of the kingdom, which belong to the Presidency of the High Priesthood. It promises blessings if the counselor is faithful in counsel, in prayer, and in preaching. It asks for prayer both vocally and in the heart, in public and in private. It tells him to succor the weak, lift up hands that hang down, and strengthen feeble knees. If he is faithful to the end, he will receive a crown of immortality and eternal life.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 81–83, “Much Is Given Much Is Required,” studies this call to a counselor in the Presidency. Whom could you “succor” or strengthen this week in the ways verse 5 lists?

contextNote.title: What a counselor’s office is for
contextNote.text: A new office raised the question of what a counselor actually does. Verse 5 answers with action: it tells the counselor to “succor the weak” and strengthen feeble knees. Verse 3 lists the duties that come first: counsel, constant prayer, and preaching. Verse 4 says that doing these things brings “the greatest good” to others. The wording of verse 5 echoes Isaiah 35:3 and Hebrews 12:12. In this passage, to “stand in the office” means lifting others, not holding rank.

passages.title: Those given much are bound by covenant to seek others’ good
passages.setting: Joseph Smith traveled to Missouri in April 1832 with Sidney Rigdon, Newel K. Whitney, and Jesse Gause. On 26 April a council of high priests and elders met in Independence. The council sustained Joseph as President of the High Priesthood. It also settled a dispute between Sidney Rigdon and Edward Partridge. Joseph dictated this revelation that afternoon, renewing the March call to form the United Firm.
passages.summary: The revelation first tells the men that as they forgive each other, the Lord forgives them. It warns that all have sinned and that much is required of those given much. It says, “I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say,” but disobedience brings no promise. It names Edward Partridge, Newel K. Whitney, Sidney Gilbert, Sidney Rigdon, Joseph Smith, John Whitmer, Oliver Cowdery, W. W. Phelps, and Martin Harris. They are to be bound by a covenant in their stewardships over the poor and the bishopric. Their work covers both Zion and Kirtland, which the revelation calls a stake to Zion. Each has equal claims on the properties by just wants and needs, and surplus goes to the Lord’s storehouse. It ends with counsel to make friends with the “mammon of unrighteousness” and leave judgment to God.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 81–83, “Much Is Given Much Is Required,” takes its title from verse 3. According to verses 17–19, what were members of the order to seek for their neighbors, and why?

contextNote.title: Why the warning comes with the forgiveness
contextNote.text: The council had just reconciled leaders who had offended each other. Verse 1 grants forgiveness, but verse 2 warns that all have sinned. Verse 3 explains the stricter standard: much given means much required. Verse 4 notes that these men had asked for and received many revelations.
