That “greater light” is why their sin brings “greater condemnation.” Verse 10 states the other side, that the Lord is bound when they obey. In this passage, accountability grows with what a person has been taught.

passages.title: Widows and orphans have a claim on the Lord’s storehouse
passages.setting: On 30 April 1832, Joseph Smith sat in council with Church leaders in Independence, Missouri. Days earlier he had visited the Colesville Saints in Kaw Township, about twelve miles west. That settlement included widows such as Phebe Peck and Anna Rogers. The Joseph Smith Papers editors think contact with these families likely raised a question. Under consecration, what claim did a widow have on property her husband had given the Church?
passages.summary: The revelation adds to the Church’s laws for women and children who have lost husbands or fathers. Wives have a claim on their husbands for support until the husbands die. Faithful widows keep fellowship in the Church; unfaithful ones lose it but may stay on their inheritances under the law of the land. Children have a claim on their parents until they come of age. After that, they have a claim on the Lord’s storehouse if their parents cannot give them inheritances. The storehouse is kept by consecrations, and it provides for widows, orphans, and the poor.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 81–83, “Much Is Given Much Is Required,” connects this section with caring for those in need. Who in verses 4–6 has a claim on the storehouse, and in what order?

contextNote.title: A widow’s land under two sets of laws
contextNote.text: Consecration raised a hard case: what if a widow’s husband had deeded their land to the Church? Verse 2 makes her fellowship depend on her own faithfulness. Verse 3 adds that even without fellowship, she “may remain upon” her inheritance. The phrase “according to the laws of the land” ties Church practice to Missouri law. Verse 6 then names the storehouse as the support for widows and orphans. In this passage, an inheritance is a family’s land that Church discipline alone does not take away.

passages.title: Priesthood ordinances make the power of godliness visible
passages.setting: Joseph Smith moved from Hiram to Kirtland, Ohio, on 12 September 1832. Elders were returning from missions in the eastern states to report on their work. Joseph inquired of the Lord with six of them, and the revelation came over the night of 22–23 September. It was probably dictated in Newel K. Whitney’s store, with Frederick G. Williams as scribe. Partway through, the text shifts to address ten high priests.
passages.summary: The revelation says the New Jerusalem and its temple will be built at the temple lot in western Missouri, within “this generation” of people. It traces the greater priesthood from Moses through Jethro, Abraham, Melchizedek, Noah, and Enoch back to Adam. It says this priesthood holds the key of the knowledge of God, and its ordinances show the power of godliness. Because Israel hardened their hearts under Moses, the higher priesthood was taken, and the lesser one continued until John the Baptist. It describes the oath and covenant of the priesthood: those who receive it receive Christ, the Father, and all the Father has. It says the whole church is under condemnation for treating lightly the Book of Mormon and the commandments. It sends the elders, called apostles and friends, to preach without purse or scrip, and warns cities that reject them. It assigns Bishop Newel K. Whitney to warn New York, Albany, and Boston, and ends with a promise of the Lord’s coming.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for section 84, “The Power of Godliness,” takes its title from verse 20. In verses 33–40, what does the Lord promise to those who receive the priesthood, and what are they asked to do?

contextNote.title: What the greater priesthood is for
contextNote.text: The revelation asks what the greater priesthood is for. Verse 19 says it holds the key of the knowledge of God. Verse 20 adds that its ordinances make “the power of godliness” manifest. Verses 21–22 state the reverse: without them, that power is not shown, and no one can see the Father and live. Verses 23–25 give Israel under Moses as the example. The people would not endure God’s presence, so the higher priesthood was taken from them. In this passage, ordinances are the means by which godly power becomes visible to people in the flesh.

passages.title: Zion’s record should list only those who keep consecration
passages.setting: Joseph Smith returned to Kirtland, Ohio, on 6 November 1832 after a trip east with Newel K. Whitney. On 27 November he wrote a letter to William W. Phelps in Independence, Missouri. Phelps had reported in print that 810 Saints had moved to Zion and asked whether all had kept the law. Some had arrived without consecrating property and so had no inheritance from the bishop. This section is an extract of that letter, printed in January 1833 and added to the Doctrine and Covenants in 1876.
passages.summary: The letter says the Lord’s clerk must keep a history and record of all that happens in Zion. The record lists those who consecrate property and receive inheritances, with their faith and works. Those who do not receive inheritances by consecration are not to be enrolled with God’s people. Their genealogy is not to be kept in the Church’s records. Joseph Smith then quotes what he calls the still small voice. It says God will send one “mighty and strong” to set the house in order and divide inheritances by lot. The man who steadies the ark will fall, and those not written in the book will have no inheritance among the Saints.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 85–87, “Stand Ye in Holy Places,” includes this letter about keeping records in Zion. Besides names, what does verse 2 say the clerk should record, and why might that matter?

contextNote.title: Why a list of names mattered
contextNote.text: Phelps faced a practical question: who counted as a settled member of Zion? Verse 1 assigns the clerk to record those who consecrate and receive inheritances. Verse 3 says those who did not consecrate should not be enrolled with God’s people. Verse 4 extends this to their genealogy in Church records. Verse 12 points to Ezra 2:61–62, where priests without a record lost their office. In this passage, being written down is a record of covenant kept, not just a count of settlers.

passages.title: The wheat is gathered before the tares are burned
passages.setting: On 6 December 1832, Joseph Smith was at Kirtland, Ohio, working on his revision of the Bible. His journal says he received a revelation that day explaining the parable of the wheat and the tares in Matthew 13. Sidney Rigdon wrote it down. It is not clear whether Joseph was then reviewing the New Testament or working on the Old Testament.
passages.summary: The revelation explains the parable of the wheat and the tares. The field is the world, and the apostles were the sowers. After the apostles died, the apostate power called Babylon sowed tares that choked the wheat and drove the church into the wilderness. In the last days the blade is springing up again, but it is still tender. Angels are ready to reap, but the Lord tells them to wait so the wheat is not destroyed. At harvest the wheat will be gathered first, and then the tares will be bound and burned. It tells priesthood holders that they are lawful heirs through the lineage of their fathers. If they continue in the Lord’s goodness, they will be a light to the Gentiles and a savior to Israel.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 85–87, “Stand Ye in Holy Places,” includes this explanation of the parable. According to verse 11, what must priesthood holders do to be a light to the Gentiles and a savior to Israel?

contextNote.title: Why the order of the harvest changes
contextNote.text: In Matthew 13:30 the tares are gathered first, then the wheat. Verse 7 reverses that order: the wheat is gathered out before the tares are bound. Verse 6 gives the reason for waiting: the blade is tender, and pulling tares now would destroy wheat too. The aside in verse 6, “your faith is weak,” shows how young the restored church was. Joseph Smith’s Bible revision of Matthew 13:30 made the same change in order. In this passage, the harvest is first a gathering of the faithful, and the burning comes after.

passages.title: War beginning in South Carolina will spread to all nations
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation on 25 December 1832 at or near Kirtland, Ohio. That autumn South Carolina had declared federal tariffs void and threatened to leave the Union. A nearby newspaper, the Painesville Telegraph, had just reported the crisis along with cholera and plague abroad. Frederick G. Williams recorded the revelation. It was left out of the 1835 and 1844 Doctrine and Covenants and first printed in England in 1851.
passages.summary: The revelation speaks of wars that will begin with the rebellion of South Carolina. It says the Southern States will be divided against the Northern States. The South will call on Great Britain, and other nations will be drawn in until war is poured out on all nations. It says slaves will rise against their masters. It says the remnants left in the land will vex the Gentiles. Famine, plague, earthquake, and lightning will follow until there is a full end of all nations. It closes by telling the Saints to stand in holy places and not be moved until the day of the Lord.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 85–87, “Stand Ye in Holy Places,” takes its title from verse 8. What places, habits, or relationships in your life could help you stand and “be not moved” as verse 8 directs?

contextNote.title: Standing still amid predicted war
contextNote.text: The revelation asks what the Saints should do while war and disaster spread. Verses 1–6 describe the danger, starting in South Carolina and widening to all nations. Verse 7 gives the stated purpose: to end the cry of the saints against their enemies. Verse 8 tells them to “stand ye in holy places” and not be moved. The command is about steadiness and place, not about joining the fighting. Latter-day Saints later pointed to the Civil War, which began in South Carolina in 1861; the 1832 crisis itself ended without war. In this passage, “holy places” are where the Saints wait for the day of the Lord.

passages.title: Light, law, and learning prepare the elders to build Zion
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at a conference of high priests in Kirtland, Ohio, on 27–28 December 1832. The elders had prayed, one by one, to learn God’s will about building Zion. His scribe wrote it down, and the original manuscript is lost. On 11 January 1833 Joseph sent a copy to William W. Phelps in Missouri and called it an “olive leaf.” Verses 127–137 come from a separate revelation of 3 January 1833 on the school of the prophets, later printed with this one.
passages.summary: The revelation tells the assembled elders their prayers were heard and promises “another Comforter.” It names the light of Christ as the power in the sun, moon, stars, and earth. That light gives life to all things and is the law that governs them. The earth will be sanctified for celestial beings, and each person receives the glory whose law he can abide. A parable of a lord visiting twelve servants, each in his hour, pictures God visiting his kingdoms. The elders must call a solemn assembly, sanctify themselves, teach one another, and seek learning “by study and also by faith.” Seven angels then sound trumpets over the Second Coming, the resurrections, and Michael’s final battle with the devil. The elders must build a house of God, and the closing verses set rules for the school of the prophets.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for section 88, “Establish … a House of God,” ties the command to build a house to holiness and learning. According to verses 119–125, what kind of people did the Lord want gathering in that house?

contextNote.title: Learning by study and by faith
contextNote.text: The elders had asked how to build Zion, and much of the answer was about learning. Verse 118 begins with a problem: “all have not faith.” Its remedy is to teach one another and to seek “out of the best books.” Verses 78–79 show how wide the subjects are, from doctrine to history, nations, and countries. Verse 80 gives the reason: the elders are being prepared to be sent out again. Verse 119 then gives the learning a place, a house that is also “a house of learning.” In this passage, seeking learning is preparation for a mission, pursued through both study and faith.

passages.title: A word of wisdom on food and drink carries a promise
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 27 February 1833. No record from the time describes the occasion. Later accounts tie it to the school of the prophets, which met at Newel K. Whitney’s store. Brigham Young, who was not present, later said tobacco use there troubled Emma Smith and others, so Joseph asked the Lord. Temperance societies were active across America and in Kirtland at the time.
passages.summary: The opening verses address the high priests in Kirtland, the church, and the Saints in Zion. They call the revelation a word of wisdom, given “not by commandment or constraint.” The voice says it warns against the designs of “conspiring men” in the last days. Wine and strong drink are not good, except homemade grape wine for the sacrament. Strong drink is for washing the body, and tobacco is for bruises and sick cattle; “hot drinks” are not for the body. Herbs, fruit, and grain are ordained for human use, and meat is to be used sparingly. Those who keep these sayings and obey are promised health, wisdom, and strength to run without weariness. The destroying angel will pass them by, as it passed ancient Israel.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 89–92, “A Principle with Promise,” presents the Word of Wisdom as care for both body and spirit. Which promises in verses 18–21 reach beyond physical health?

contextNote.title: A principle fitted to the weakest Saint
contextNote.text: Verse 2 says the revelation came “not by commandment or constraint.” So why would members keep it? Verse 3 answers by calling it “a principle with promise.” It is also fitted to “the weakest of all saints,” so no one is beyond its reach. Verses 18–21 spell out the promise: health, hidden knowledge, endurance, and protection. The promise depends on keeping these sayings while “walking in obedience to the commandments.” Here, a principle with promise is counsel that carries its own reward for those who follow it.

passages.title: Two counselors share the keys and the work of presiding
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 8 March 1833. Jesse Gause, one of his counselors, had been excommunicated in December 1832. Frederick G. Williams was called in January 1833 to take his place. The revelation advanced the presidency of the high priesthood, and the counselors were ordained on 18 March. Leaders in Kirtland and Missouri were also in tension over Zion at the time.
passages.summary: The revelation forgives Joseph Smith and confirms his keys, through which “the oracles” go to the church. Sidney Rigdon and Frederick G. Williams are forgiven and made equal with Joseph in holding these keys. The three are to finish translating the prophets, then preside over the church and school, study, and learn languages. Joseph Smith Sr. and Sidney Rigdon stay where they live, Williams needs a home, and the bishop must find an agent to clear debts. Vienna Jaques is to receive money for her journey and an inheritance in Zion. The Lord is displeased with William E. McLellin and Sidney Gilbert, and the bishop and others must repent. Zion will be chastened, yet not removed from her place.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 89–92 includes this revelation on the presidency of the Church. What warning does verse 5 give to those who receive “the oracles of God,” and what storms does it name?

contextNote.title: Keys shared without losing the order
contextNote.text: After Jesse Gause left, the presidency needed to be settled. Verse 6 says Rigdon and Williams are “equal with thee in holding the keys.” Verse 4 shows that an order remains: the oracles come “through you” to the church. Verses 12–16 then give the three a shared task, to preside in council and set the church in order. The JSP notes that Joseph Smith kept the presiding role after this revelation. Here, equal in the keys means sharing authority to lead in council, while revelation still comes through Joseph.

passages.title: The Apocrypha helps only the reader the Spirit enlightens
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 9 March 1833. He was revising the Bible and had finished the New Testament in February. He had reached the Apocrypha, books outside the Hebrew canon that some Bibles then included. He asked the Lord whether to revise those books too. Some Bible societies had recently stopped printing Bibles that contained them.
passages.summary: The revelation answers a question about the Apocrypha. It says many things in those books are true and mostly translated correctly. It also says many things in them are not true but were added by human hands. The Apocrypha does not need to be translated. Whoever reads it should read with understanding, because “the Spirit manifesteth truth.” A reader enlightened by the Spirit will benefit, and one who is not will not.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 89–92 includes this short revelation on the Apocrypha. How could the test in verses 4–6 guide your reading of other books that mix truth and error?

contextNote.title: The Spirit as the reader’s filter
contextNote.text: The question was practical: should the revision include these extra books? Verses 1–2 give a mixed verdict, with truth and error side by side. Verse 3 settles the task by saying translation is “not needful.” Verse 4 shifts the work to the reader, because “the Spirit manifesteth truth.” Verses 5–6 state the result both ways: enlightened readers benefit, and others do not. In this passage, to understand means to tell true from false by the Spirit, not by a corrected edition.

passages.title: Frederick G. Williams joins the United Firm as a lively member
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 15 March 1833. A week earlier, Frederick G. Williams had been named to the presidency with Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon. He had worked for the United Firm as a paid assistant scribe since January. The firm managed the church’s printing, stores, and properties in Kirtland and Missouri.
passages.summary: The revelation is addressed to the united order, also called the United Firm. It tells the members to receive Frederick G. Williams into the order. It adds that what is said to one is said to all. Then it speaks to Williams himself. He is to be “a lively member” of the order. If he keeps all former commandments, he will be blessed forever.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 89–92 includes this call to Frederick G. Williams. Verse 1 says what is said to one is said to all; what would being “a lively member” look like in your ward?

contextNote.title: What a lively member owes
contextNote.text: Williams already served the firm, but only as a paid scribe. Verse 1 changes his standing by receiving him into the order itself. The JSP notes that firm members were to be equal partners with equal claims on its property. Verse 2 then asks him to be “a lively member,” an active partner rather than a name on a list. The promise in verse 2 depends on faithfulness to “all former commandments.” Here, lively means engaged and faithful in the firm’s shared work.

passages.title: Christ received grace for grace, and so may his followers
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 6 May 1833, and few sources describe its background. Part of it is addressed to Frederick G. Williams, Sidney Rigdon, and Newel K. Whitney. Whitney’s note on his copy called it a reprimand about their families, though most of the text concerns the Father and the Son. Its opening echoes John 1, but the JSP judges it separate from the New Testament revision finished in February 1833.
passages.summary: The revelation promises that those who forsake sin and obey will see Christ’s face and know that he is. It then quotes a record of John, who saw that Christ “received not of the fulness at first.” Christ continued “from grace to grace” until he received a fulness of the Father’s glory. Those who keep the commandments may also receive grace for grace and come to the Father’s fulness. The revelation says people were with God in the beginning, and that intelligence was not created. It defines truth as knowledge of things as they are, were, and will be, and calls God’s glory “light and truth.” Williams and Rigdon are rebuked for not teaching their children, and Joseph Smith and Whitney must set their families in order. Rigdon is to go on his journey and preach, and Joseph and Williams are to make haste also. All are to hasten the translation and study history and law.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for section 93, “Receive of His Fulness,” teaches that we can grow as the Savior did. According to verses 12–20 and 28, what moves a person from one degree of grace to the next?

contextNote.title: Grace for grace as a pattern of growth
contextNote.text: Verse 19 names the need the revelation answers: to “know how to worship, and know what you worship.” Verses 12–13 answer by describing how Christ himself grew. He “received not of the fulness at first” but “continued from grace to grace.” Verse 20 applies the same pattern to the hearers: keep the commandments, and “you shall receive grace for grace.” Verse 28 restates it as receiving truth and light until one “knoweth all things.” In this passage, grace for grace names gradual growth, step by step, toward the Father’s fulness.

passages.title: Kirtland is laid out as a stake around the Lord’s house
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 2 August 1833. Earlier editions dated it 6 May 1833, an error corrected in the 2013 edition. That spring the church had bought Peter French’s farm, where the Lord’s house would stand at the center of the city plat. In the same weeks the presidency drafted plans for Kirtland and for Zion in Missouri. Kirtland leaders did not yet know that a mob in Independence had destroyed the church’s press in July.
passages.summary: The revelation commands the Saints to lay out Kirtland as the “city of the stake of Zion,” starting from the Lord’s house. The work must follow the pattern already given. The first lot south is for a house for the presidency, fifty-five by sixty-five feet, with lower and higher courts. It must be kept clean, or the Lord’s glory and presence will not be there. The second lot south is for a house of the same size for printing the scripture translation. Hyrum Smith, Reynolds Cahoon, and Jared Carter receive lots and are named a committee to build the houses. The two houses are not to be built until a later commandment.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 94–97 uses this section to teach that we can be “wholly dedicated unto the Lord.” What do verses 8–9 suggest about keeping a place, or a life, fit for the Lord’s presence?

contextNote.title: A holy house at the center of the city
contextNote.text: The Saints were planning a city, and verse 1 says to begin “at my house.” Verses 3 and 10 then place two more buildings beside it, for the presidency and for printing. Verse 8 sets the condition for the presidency’s house: no unclean thing may enter. If that holds, the voice says, “my glory shall be there, and my presence shall be there.” Verse 9 states the reverse: if uncleanness comes in, his presence will not. In this passage, a dedicated house is one kept clean so that God’s presence can remain.

passages.title: The Lord rebukes the delay in building his house
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 1 June 1833. Revelations in December 1832 and January 1833 had commanded a house of the Lord and a school. In May a conference named Hyrum Smith, Reynolds Cahoon, and Jared Carter to raise funds for it. Nearly a month later, no one had begun to build. A council then appointed Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Frederick G. Williams to plan the inner court, and work began by 7 June.
passages.summary: The revelation opens by saying the Lord chastens those he loves to prepare their deliverance. It rebukes them for a “very grievous sin”: neglecting the command to build the house meant to prepare his apostles. Many have been called, but few chosen, and those not chosen walk “in darkness at noon-day.” The voice says the chosen will be endowed with power from on high in this house. They must tarry, as the apostles did at Jerusalem. It also names contention in the school of the prophets as grievous. The house is to be built not after the world’s manner but by a pattern shown to three men. It will measure fifty-five by sixty-five feet, with a lower court for worship and a higher court for the apostles’ school.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 94–97, “For the Salvation of Zion,” connects this revelation with the blessings promised in the Lord’s house. According to verses 1–2 and 8–9, what was the Lord offering the Saints through this rebuke?

contextNote.title: Why the house could not wait
contextNote.text: The Saints had the command but had not begun to build. Verse 3 calls the delay a “very grievous sin.” Verse 8 explains why it mattered: in this house the Lord would “endow” the chosen “with power from on high.” Verse 9 compares this to the apostles at Jerusalem, who were told to wait for promised power. Verse 11 adds the condition: keeping the commandments brings “power to build it.” In this passage, to endow means to give power to those being prepared for the ministry.

passages.title: The French farm is assigned to strengthen Kirtland as a stake
passages.setting: High priests met on 4 June 1833 in the translating room of Newel K. Whitney’s store in Kirtland, Ohio. The church had recently bought the 103-acre farm of Peter French. The council could not agree on who should manage it, so they agreed to ask the Lord. Joseph Smith dictated this revelation during the meeting. That same day, the council put Whitney in charge of the farm and admitted John Johnson to the United Firm.
passages.summary: The revelation says this stake, set “for the strength of Zion,” must be made strong. Newel K. Whitney is to take charge of the place where the Lord’s house will be built. The land is to be divided into lots for those seeking inheritances, as the council decides. A portion is to serve the order’s purpose of bringing forth the Lord’s word. The voice calls the spread of that word “most expedient,” to subdue people’s hearts. John Johnson’s offering is accepted, and he is promised eternal life if he keeps the commandments. He is called a descendant of Joseph and is to join the order. He is to remove the debts on “the house named among you” so that he may live there.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 94–97, “For the Salvation of Zion,” treats Kirtland’s growth as part of building Zion. How do verses 1 and 5 tie a practical decision about land to the spread of the Lord’s word?

contextNote.title: Land managed so the word can go out
contextNote.text: The council disagreed over a piece of land, and the answer turned to its purpose. Verse 2 gives Whitney charge of the place chosen for the Lord’s house. Verse 4 reserves part of the land for the order’s work of “bringing forth my word.” Verse 5 calls this work “the most expedient,” so that hearts may be subdued. Verse 8 gives the same reason for adding John Johnson to the order. In this passage, expedient means the most needed use, the one that serves the spread of the Lord’s word.

passages.title: Zion’s safety depends on a pure people and a holy house
passages.setting: Church members in Jackson County, Missouri, had formed a school of the prophets in the summer of 1833. Parley P. Pratt taught a class of about sixty men there each week. In early July, Oliver Cowdery and the school wrote to Joseph Smith in Kirtland, asking him to inquire about the school. Joseph dictated this revelation on 2 August and sent it to Missouri in a letter of 6 August. He did not yet know that a mob had attacked the Saints in Independence in late July.
passages.summary: The revelation speaks to Joseph Smith about the Saints in Zion, many of whom are humble and seeking wisdom. It approves the school in Zion and Parley P. Pratt as its leader, as long as he abides in the Lord. Others in the school must be chastened, but the honest and contrite who keep their covenants by sacrifice are accepted. It then commands that a house be built in Zion, quickly, by the tithing of the people. The house is for thanksgiving and for instructing those called to the ministry. If it is kept undefiled, the Lord’s glory and presence will be there, and the pure in heart will see God. The revelation defines Zion as “the pure in heart.” Zion will escape coming judgments if she obeys, but will suffer if she does not.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson “For the Salvation of Zion” covers sections 94–97. It teaches that Zion is the pure in heart and that temples are places of instruction and of God’s presence. According to verses 13–16, what purposes does the Lord give for His house, and what does He ask of those who enter?

contextNote.title: Zion defined by its people
contextNote.text: The Missouri Saints wanted guidance about their school and their future in Zion. Verse 21 answers by defining Zion as “the pure in heart,” not first as a piece of land. Verses 15–17 apply the same test to the planned house: the Lord’s glory will rest there only if it is not defiled. Verse 16 promises that “the pure in heart” who enter it “shall see God.” Verses 25–26 then make Zion’s safety conditional on obedience. In this passage, purity is the condition that turns a place into Zion.

passages.title: Bear persecution patiently, forgive, and renounce war
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 6 August 1833. Two weeks earlier, a mob in Independence, Missouri, had destroyed the Church printing office and tarred and feathered Bishop Edward Partridge and Charles Allen. On 23 July, Church leaders there agreed under pressure to leave Jackson County. The official heading says Joseph could have known the seriousness of events only by revelation. The Joseph Smith Papers notes the text never names Jackson County and may also reflect rising opposition in Kirtland. It was copied into a letter to Missouri the same day.
passages.summary: The revelation tells the Saints not to fear, to give thanks, and to wait on the Lord. It promises that their afflictions will work together for their good. It says the constitutional law that protects freedom is justified, and that honest and wise leaders should be sought. It calls the Saints to renounce war and proclaim peace. It rebukes many in the Kirtland church for pride and covetousness. Then it gives a law for enduring attacks: bear the first, second, and third offense patiently. After warning an enemy, the injured may be justified in defending themselves. It also gives an ancient pattern of offering peace three times before war, It commands forgiveness of a repentant enemy every time. An unrepentant enemy is forgiven three times, and the fourth offense is brought before the Lord.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson “Be Still and Know That I Am God” covers sections 98–101. It teaches that the Lord asks His people to seek peace and to trust that afflictions can work for their good. How do verses 23–27 and 39–40 describe the way to respond when someone wrongs you repeatedly?

contextNote.title: Peace offered before any defense
contextNote.text: The Saints faced violence and had to decide how to respond. Verse 16 sets the main direction, telling them to “renounce war and proclaim peace.” Verses 23–27 explain what that means under attack. Each offense borne patiently brings a greater reward and stands as a testimony against the attacker. Verses 33–36 give the same pattern for nations: lift a standard of peace three times before any battle. Verses 39–40 add that a repentant enemy must always be forgiven. In this passage, renouncing war means exhausting peace first, not merely avoiding fights.

passages.title: A lifelong mission call, after the children are cared for
passages.setting: John Murdock joined the Church in Ohio in November 1830 and gave himself to preaching. His wife, Julia Clapp, died in April 1831 after giving birth to twins. Joseph and Emma Smith adopted the twins, and other families cared for his older children. One twin died in March 1832 after the mob attack on the Johnson home in Hiram. Murdock returned to Ohio sick that summer. Joseph Smith dictated this revelation for him at Hiram on 29 August 1832.
passages.summary: The revelation calls John Murdock to preach in the eastern countries. He is to go from house to house, village to village, and city to city, amid persecution. Those who receive him receive the Lord, and he will speak with the power of the Spirit. Those who reject him will be rejected, and he is to cleanse his feet as a testimony against them. He is not to leave until his children are provided for and sent kindly to the bishop in Zion. After a few years he may go to Zion for his inheritance, if he wishes. Otherwise he is to keep preaching until he is taken.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 98–101 includes this call to John Murdock, a father who sacrificed to serve. What do verses 2–3 promise Murdock as he preaches, and how might verse 6 shape how you balance service and family?

contextNote.title: Family care comes before the mission
contextNote.text: Murdock was a widowed father whose children were scattered among other families. Verse 6 answers the obvious question: he must not leave until his children are provided for. The children are to be sent “kindly” to the bishop in Zion. Only then does the broad call of verse 1 take effect. Verses 7–8 then give him a choice between settling in Zion later or preaching for life. In this passage, provision for the children is a stated condition of the call, not an afterthought.

passages.title: God keeps the families while the missionaries speak
passages.setting: Freeman and Huldah Nickerson of Perrysburg, New York, came to Kirtland in September 1833. They asked Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon to preach to their family in New York and Upper Canada. Joseph and Sidney left Kirtland with them on 5 October. They reached the Nickerson home in Perrysburg on 12 October, worried about the families they had left. This revelation was recorded there that day. The two then went on to preach and baptize in Upper Canada.
passages.summary: The revelation tells Sidney Rigdon and Joseph Smith that their families are well and in the Lord’s hands. It says the Lord has many people in this region, and an effectual door will open. They are to speak what is put into their hearts, in solemnity and meekness. The Holy Ghost will bear record of what they say. Sidney is called as a spokesman for Joseph, and Joseph is to be a revelator to Sidney. It promises that Zion will be redeemed, though chastened for a season. Orson Hyde and John Gould are in the Lord’s hands. All things will work together for good to the upright.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 98–101 uses sections 99–100 to teach that the Lord takes care of people who serve him. According to verses 5–8, what must Joseph and Sidney do so that the Holy Ghost will bear record of their words?

contextNote.title: Words given in the moment
contextNote.text: Joseph and Sidney were far from home, about to preach to strangers. Verse 5 tells them to speak the thoughts the Lord will put into their hearts. Verse 6 gives the reason they need not prepare in fear: the words will be given “in the very hour” they are needed. Verse 7 sets the manner, in solemnity of heart and meekness. Verse 8 promises that the Holy Ghost will then bear record of their words. In this passage, being given words depends on speaking in the right spirit.

passages.title: Zion is chastened but not moved from her place
passages.setting: In late October and early November 1833, armed residents drove the Latter-day Saints out of Jackson County, Missouri. Two attackers died in a clash on 4 November, and a militia then disarmed the Saints. Most refugees crossed into Clay County, losing homes, goods, livestock, and crops. In Kirtland, Joseph Smith heard reports from Orson Hyde and John Gould and letters from Edward Partridge and others. Joseph dictated this revelation on 16–17 December 1833. The earliest known copy is undated; later copies give these dates.
passages.summary: The revelation says the Lord allowed the affliction because of the Saints’ transgressions, naming contention, envy, and covetous desires. Yet it promises compassion and says the Lord will not cast them off. Zion will not be moved, and the pure in heart will return to build its waste places. It describes the day of the Lord’s coming, when enmity ends and all things are revealed. A parable tells of a nobleman’s servants who neglected to build a watchtower and lost the vineyard. The lord then sends a servant to gather the strength of his house and redeem it. The churches are to keep gathering, buy land in Jackson County, and not sell their claims there. The Saints are to petition the judge, the governor, and the president, under a Constitution the text says God established. Sidney Gilbert is told not to sell the storehouse.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson “Be Still and Know That I Am God” covers sections 98–101. It teaches that the Lord can comfort His people in trial. What reasons for hope do verses 9–18 give the scattered Saints?

contextNote.title: Stillness without explanation
contextNote.text: The exiled Saints wanted to know why they had suffered and how they would return. Joseph had written to them that the Lord’s only answer so far was to be still. Verse 16 repeats that counsel, and its reason is that “all flesh is in mine hands” already. Verse 17 joins this to a promise that Zion will not be moved out of her place. Verses 86–89 show that stillness did not mean doing nothing, since the Saints were to petition for redress. In this passage, being still means trusting God’s control while still acting lawfully.

passages.title: A standing council gives the accused a fair hearing
passages.setting: On 17 February 1834, twenty-four high priests met at Joseph Smith’s house in Kirtland, Ohio. They organized a standing high council to settle serious disputes the Church or a bishop’s council could not resolve. Clerk Orson Hyde noted that some errors were likely made, and the meeting asked Joseph to correct them. Joseph revised the minutes the next day. On 19 February the council accepted them unanimously as its form and constitution. Verses 30–32, about the Twelve Apostles, were added in 1835.
passages.summary: These are minutes, not a revelation in the Lord’s voice. They record the organizing of a high council of twelve high priests, with one or three presidents. Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Frederick Williams are acknowledged as presidents. Twelve councilors are chosen, including Joseph Smith’s father, Martin Harris, and Oliver Cowdery. The minutes set a quorum of seven, a way to fill vacancies, and an order for speaking by drawn numbers. Half the council stands for the accused, and the president decides with the council’s vote or a rehearing. Traveling high priests may form councils abroad, with appeal to the high council at the First Presidency’s seat.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 102–105 uses verses 12–23 to ask what membership councils are for. How do verses 15–22 protect both the accused and the truth of the case?

contextNote.title: Half the council for the accused
contextNote.text: The new council needed a way to judge disputes without bias. Verse 15 gives the accused a right to one-half of the council. The stated purpose is to prevent insult or injustice. Verse 17 makes this concrete: councilors drawing even numbers speak for the accused. Verse 18 then lets both accuser and accused speak for themselves. In these minutes, fairness is built into the seating and speaking order, not left to goodwill.

passages.title: Zion’s redemption requires volunteers, means, and obedience
passages.setting: Two Missouri leaders, Parley Pratt and Lyman Wight, arrived in Kirtland on 24 February 1834. They reported to the Kirtland high council on the exiled Saints, most of them in Clay County. They asked how Zion would be redeemed. At that meeting Joseph Smith offered to lead an expedition, and thirty or forty others volunteered. Joseph dictated this revelation the same day, but records do not show whether before, during, or after the meeting.
passages.summary: The revelation tells the Lord’s “friends” how to act for their scattered brethren in Zion. It says the Saints were chastened because they did not fully obey. If they now hearken, they will begin to prevail. If not, the world will prevail against them. The scattered will return and build up Zion, but only if they do not pollute their inheritances. Zion’s redemption must come by power, led by a man like Moses. Joseph Smith is named as the servant in the earlier parable of the vineyard. He is to gather the young and middle-aged men to Zion. Pairs of recruiters are sent out to seek five hundred men, and no fewer than one hundred.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 102–105, “After Much Tribulation … Cometh the Blessing,” draws from verse 12 that blessings can follow trials. What conditions do verses 5–8 and 36 attach to the promised victory, and how might they apply to a blessing you are seeking?

contextNote.title: Redemption tied to hearkening
contextNote.text: The exiles wanted to know how they could return to Jackson County. Verse 15 says Zion’s redemption must come by power. Verses 5–8 first set the condition: the Saints will prevail only if they hearken from that very hour. Verse 14 adds that even restored lands can be lost if they are polluted. Verses 31–34 show the same pattern in recruiting, asking for five hundred but allowing fewer. In this passage, power to redeem Zion is promised, but always on condition of obedience.

passages.title: Everything belongs to God, so the owners are stewards
passages.setting: The United Firm was formed in 1832 to run the Church’s stores and printing. By 1834 it was deep in debt, and the Missouri store and press had been lost to mob violence. Some members were accused of treating firm property as their own. On 10 April 1834 the Kirtland members voted to dissolve the firm. This revelation, given at or near Kirtland on 23 April, instead reorganized it. The 1835 edition later used substitute names and called it the “United Order.”
passages.summary: The revelation addresses the order the Lord commanded to be organized. It says some members broke the covenant through covetousness and feigned words, and are cursed. Members are to be organized and each given a stewardship to account for. It says the earth is the Lord’s, there is enough and to spare, and the poor are to be exalted. It assigns Kirtland properties to Sidney Rigdon, Martin Harris, Frederick Williams, Oliver Cowdery, John Johnson, Newel Whitney, and Joseph Smith. The Kirtland and Missouri branches are separated. Two treasuries are created, one for the sacred writings and one for stewardship income. Members are to pay their debts and write to New York, and may pledge their properties this once.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 102–105 teaches from this revelation that we are stewards over what God has given us. What do verses 13–18 say about who owns the earth and how its abundance should reach the poor?

contextNote.title: Stewards, not owners
contextNote.text: The firm’s members had begun to treat shared property as their own. Verse 56 answers with a plain test: if the properties are the Lord’s, then the holders are stewards. Verse 55 states the premise that all these properties belong to the Lord. Verse 14 gives the reason, since the Lord made the earth and all things in it. Verse 70 applies this to money, which no one may call his own. In this passage, a steward holds and uses property but must account for it.

passages.title: Zion’s redemption waits for a prepared, endowed people
passages.setting: Joseph Smith led an armed expedition, later called Zion’s Camp, from Ohio to Missouri in May and June 1834. It aimed to help Saints driven from Jackson County regain their lands. Governor Daniel Dunklin did not call out the militia to escort them, and a Clay County delegation warned of violence. On 22 June 1834, at a campsite about four miles north of Fishing River, Joseph dictated this revelation. Soon after, the camp disbanded, and cholera struck many members.
passages.summary: The revelation, addressed to those gathered, says Zion could have been redeemed already but for the church’s transgressions. It names disobedience, failure to share with the poor, and lack of union, mainly among the churches abroad. It says the elders must wait “for a little season” and first be “endowed with power from on high.” That endowment is to come in the house being built in Kirtland. It says the Lord will fight Zion’s battles and accepts the offering of those who came. Those who can stay in the region should stay; those with families in the east are to follow Joseph’s direction. The Saints are to buy land in Jackson County and nearby counties, gather quietly, and not boast. It closes by telling them to “sue for peace” with all people.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 102–105 presents Zion’s Camp as a trial that prepared faithful disciples. What do verses 3–6 suggest about the kind of people who can build Zion?

contextNote.title: Waiting as a season of preparation
contextNote.text: The camp had marched hundreds of miles and now would not enter Jackson County. Verse 9 says the elders must wait for Zion’s redemption. Verse 10 gives the reason: so they may be prepared and taught more perfectly. Verse 11 adds that this cannot happen until they are “endowed with power from on high.” Verse 33 places that endowment in the house commanded in Kirtland. Verses 3–4 explain why preparation was lacking: the Saints were not united and did not care for the poor. In this passage, waiting means a season of training before Zion’s redemption is pursued again.

passages.title: A humbled convert is called to preside and preach in Freedom
passages.setting: Warren A. Cowdery, an older brother of Oliver Cowdery, lived in Freedom, New York. He had corresponded with Oliver in Kirtland and was not yet a member in spring 1834. Joseph Smith dictated this revelation for him at Kirtland on 25 November 1834. Freedom served as a gathering point for several branches in western New York.
passages.summary: The revelation calls Warren A. Cowdery to be ordained a presiding high priest over the church in Freedom and nearby areas. He is to preach and warn people there and in adjoining counties. He is to give his whole time to the calling, and the text says “the laborer is worthy of his hire.” It warns that the Lord’s coming will overtake the world “as a thief in the night.” Those who are “children of light” need not be caught off guard. It says heaven rejoiced when Warren turned from “the crafts of men.” Despite “the vanity of his heart,” he will be lifted up if he humbles himself. If he stays a faithful witness, a crown is prepared for him.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 106–108 includes this call to Warren Cowdery as an example of the Lord calling imperfect people. How do verses 7–8 balance Warren’s weakness with the Lord’s promises?

contextNote.title: Mercy paired with a frank warning
contextNote.text: The revelation calls a new convert to lead, yet it names a fault in him. Verse 6 says heaven rejoiced when Warren “bowed to my scepter.” Verse 7 then admits “the vanity of his heart” in the same breath as mercy. The promise is conditional: he will be lifted up “inasmuch as he will humble himself.” Verse 8 adds grace “wherewith he may stand” and a crown if he stays faithful. In this passage, being lifted up depends on Warren choosing humility, not on being free of the fault.

passages.title: Priesthood order rests on councils, keys, and learning one’s duty
passages.setting: In February and March 1835, the church organized the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and the first Seventy. The Twelve were preparing to leave Kirtland on 4 May 1835 for conferences in the eastern states. Joseph Smith gave them this instruction on priesthood sometime between about 1 March and 4 May. Most of verses 60–100 draws on a revelation he dictated in November 1831. It was printed as “On Priesthood” in the 1835 Doctrine and Covenants.
passages.summary: The instruction says the church has two priesthoods, the Melchizedek and the Aaronic. It explains their names and gives each priesthood its keys and duties. It sets out presiding quorums: the Presidency of the Church, the Twelve, and the Seventy. Their decisions must be unanimous and made in righteousness, with appeal possible when a decision is unrighteous. It traces a patriarchal order from Adam through Noah and describes Adam’s last blessing at Adam-ondi-Ahman. Then it details bishops and church councils, including a council that can try the church president. It gives quorum sizes and presidents for deacons, teachers, priests, elders, and the Seventy. It ends: “let every man learn his duty” and act “in all diligence.”

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 106–108 takes its title, “The Order of the Son of God,” from verse 3. What do verses 85–89 ask quorum presidents to do, and how does that serve the command in verse 99?

contextNote.title: Order ends in personal duty
contextNote.text: After listing offices, quorums, and councils, the instruction turns to each person. Verse 99 tells “every man” to learn his duty and act in his office. Verse 100 gives the result of neglect: the slothful “shall not be counted worthy to stand.” The long lists before it supply much of what there is to learn. Verses 85–89, for example, describe presidents who teach their quorums their duties. Verse 99 makes that teaching useful only when it is acted on. In this passage, “duty” means the specific work of one’s own office, learned and then done.

passages.title: A troubled Seventy is told to rest and wait
passages.setting: Lyman Sherman joined the church in New York in 1832 and moved to Kirtland in 1833. He marched with Zion’s Camp and was called in February 1835 as one of seven presidents of the Seventy. On 26 December 1835 he visited Joseph Smith, who was studying Hebrew. Sherman said he had been promised a revelation that would make known his duty. Joseph dictated this response that day, likely with Frederick G. Williams as scribe.
passages.summary: The revelation tells Lyman that his sins are forgiven because he came that morning to seek counsel. It tells him to let his soul rest about his spiritual standing and to resist the Lord’s voice no more. He should keep his vows more carefully and will be greatly blessed. He is to wait for the solemn assembly. Then he will be remembered with the first elders and ordained with them. From that time he will have right to preach wherever he is sent. He is to strengthen his brethren in conversation, prayer, exhortation, and action. The Lord promises to be with him to bless and deliver him.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 106–108 cites verse 7 to teach that the Lord supports those he calls to serve. What does verse 7 ask of Lyman, and how might it follow from the peace offered in verse 2?

contextNote.title: Rest that comes from obeying a prompting
contextNote.text: Sherman came worried about his standing and his duty. Verse 1 links forgiveness to a simple act: he obeyed “in coming up hither this morning.” Verse 2 then tells him to “let your soul be at rest.” The same verse adds “resist no more my voice,” suggesting he had held back before. Verse 7 turns that rest outward, asking him to strengthen his brethren. In this passage, rest is settled confidence about his standing, given so he can serve others.

passages.title: A temple prayer asks God to accept and fill his house
passages.setting: Latter-day Saints in Kirtland, Ohio, had worked since 1833 to build the House of the Lord. On 26 March 1836, Joseph Smith met with Oliver Cowdery, Sidney Rigdon, and scribes to prepare the dedicatory prayer. The official heading says the prayer was given to them by revelation. It was printed overnight so Joseph could read it. On 27 March 1836, he read it to about 1,000 people, who accepted it by vote.
passages.summary: The prayer thanks God and asks him to accept the house the Saints built through poverty and tribulation. It repeats the earlier command to build a house of prayer, fasting, faith, learning, glory, and order. It asks that God’s glory and presence rest there and that all who enter feel his power. It asks that servants go out armed with power and that enemies and lying reports fail. It pleads for the Saints driven from Jackson County, Missouri. It asks mercy for nations and rulers, the Constitution’s preservation, and the redemption of Jerusalem and scattered Israel. It remembers Joseph Smith, his family, the church presidents, and the whole church. It closes by asking God to accept the dedication, with the cry “Hosanna to God and the Lamb!”

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 109–110 takes its title, “It Is Thy House, a Place of Thy Holiness,” from verse 13. What blessings do verses 22–23 ask for those who leave the temple?

contextNote.title: A house others can recognize as holy
contextNote.text: The Saints had built the house in poverty and now asked what would make it more than a building. Verse 12 asks that God’s glory and “holy presence” rest there continually. Verse 13 asks that all who cross the threshold “may feel thy power.” They would then acknowledge “that it is thy house, a place of thy holiness.” Verse 20 adds that “no unclean thing” may enter to pollute it. In this prayer, holiness is God’s presence felt by those who enter, guarded by the people’s worthiness.

passages.title: Christ accepts the temple and ancient prophets restore keys
passages.setting: One week after the dedication, on Easter Sunday, 3 April 1836, the Saints met in the Kirtland temple. After the sacrament, Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery withdrew behind lowered veils at the pulpit to pray in silence. Warren A. Cowdery recorded their account in Joseph’s journal in the third person. Willard Richards later recast it in the first person, and it entered the Doctrine and Covenants in 1876.
passages.summary: The account says the veil was taken from the minds of Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery. They report seeing the Lord standing on the pulpit, with eyes like fire and a voice like rushing waters. He declares their sins forgiven and says he has accepted the house. He promises to appear there if his people keep it holy, and says its fame will spread. Then Moses appears and commits the keys of gathering Israel and leading the ten tribes. Elias commits the dispensation of the gospel of Abraham. Elijah appears last, saying the time Malachi spoke of has fully come. He commits keys tied to turning the hearts of fathers and children to each other.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 109–110 connects these visions to temple blessings. What keys are named in verses 11–16, and what work does each one point to?

contextNote.title: An answer to the dedicatory prayer
contextNote.text: One week earlier, the dedicatory prayer had asked God to accept the house. Verse 7 reports the answer in direct speech: “I have accepted this house.” The voice adds “my name shall be here” and promises to appear in mercy. Verse 8 sets a condition: the people must keep the commandments and not pollute it. The keys in verses 11–16 come only after this acceptance. In this account, acceptance means the house becomes a place where the Lord says he will show himself.

passages.title: After an uncertain errand, the travelers are told not to worry
passages.setting: The church carried heavy debts from building the Kirtland temple and buying land in Ohio and Missouri. In late July 1836, Joseph Smith, Hyrum Smith, Oliver Cowdery, and Sidney Rigdon traveled east, staying in Salem, Massachusetts, from 5 August. The official heading says they had heard that a large sum of money might be available there. No contemporary record states their reasons, and no money came of the trip. The revelation is dated 6 August 1836.
passages.summary: The revelation says the Lord is “not displeased” with the journey, despite their “follies.” It says there is much treasure in Salem for Zion, and people to gather in due time. It tells them to form acquaintances with men in the city. It promises the city and its gold and silver will be theirs in due time. It tells them not to worry about their debts or about Zion. They should stay in the area, and the Spirit’s peace will show where. They are to inquire about the city’s early inhabitants and founders. It ends with counsel to be “wise as serpents” and a promise to “order all things for your good.”

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 111–114 takes its title, “I Will Order All Things for Your Good,” from verse 11. What might “more treasures than one” in verse 10 have meant for these men?

contextNote.title: Correction without condemnation
contextNote.text: The men had come east under pressure from debt, with uncertain hopes. Verse 1 opens by naming their “follies” but says the Lord is not displeased. Verses 5–6 lift two burdens: their debts and their worry for Zion. Verse 10 says there are “more treasures than one” in the city. Verse 11 then asks them to be wise yet “without sin.” It promises to order things “as fast as ye are able to receive them.” In this passage, the Lord’s ordering is gradual and fits what they can receive.

passages.title: The Twelve must be humble and follow the First Presidency
passages.setting: In 1837, many church members in Kirtland, including some apostles, turned against Joseph Smith’s leadership. Thomas B. Marsh, president of the Quorum of the Twelve, came from Far West, Missouri, in July to reconcile the quorum. He had also been troubled that some apostles planned missions abroad without consulting him. In June, Heber C. Kimball and Orson Hyde had left to preach in England. Joseph Smith dictated this revelation to Marsh at Kirtland on 23 July 1837.
passages.summary: The revelation tells Thomas B. Marsh that his prayers and alms for the Twelve are heard. It says some things in his heart displeased the Lord, but his sins are forgiven because he humbled himself. He is to bear record to Gentiles and Jews and keep his home in Zion. It tells him to be humble, pray for the Twelve, and admonish them sharply. The Lord says he will heal them if they do not harden their hearts. The Twelve are told not to rebel against Joseph, who keeps the keys until the Lord comes. Marsh holds the keys of the kingdom for the Twelve abroad, under the First Presidency. It warns that judgment will begin at the Lord’s house and calls the Twelve to purify their hearts.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 111–114 includes this revelation’s counsel on humility and unity among the Twelve. What do verses 11–13 ask Marsh to feel and do toward his struggling brethren?

contextNote.title: Humility as the condition for leading
contextNote.text: Marsh led a quorum divided by dissent, and he had his own grievance. Verse 3 forgives him “inasmuch as thou hast abased thyself.” Verse 10 makes humility the way forward: “Be thou humble.” The promised result is that the Lord will “lead thee by the hand” and answer his prayers. Verse 15 gives the whole quorum the same warning: “Exalt not yourselves.” In this passage, humility means accepting direction through Joseph and the First Presidency, not acting alone.

passages.title: Isaiah’s stem, rod, and root point to Christ and latter-day servants
passages.setting: Joseph Smith arrived at Far West, Missouri, in mid-March 1838 after leaving Kirtland. Between about 16 and 29 March, he answered questions about Isaiah 11 and Isaiah 52. An unnamed person asked the first three; Elias Higbee, a Caldwell County judge and high councilor, asked the others. George W. Robinson later copied both sets into Joseph’s Scriptory Book. They were first combined and published in 1853.
passages.summary: The section is a set of questions and answers on Isaiah. It says the Stem of Jesse in Isaiah 11 is Christ. The rod is a servant in Christ’s hands, descended from Jesse and from Ephraim. The root of Jesse is a descendant of Jesse and Joseph who holds priesthood and keys for the gathering. Elias Higbee then asks about Isaiah 52’s command, “Put on thy strength, O Zion.” The answer says this means putting on priesthood authority, which Zion has a right to by lineage. Zion loosing the bands from her neck means scattered Israel returning to the Lord.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 111–114 includes these answers about Isaiah. According to verses 7–8, what does it mean for Zion to “put on thy strength”?

contextNote.title: Zion’s strength is priesthood authority
contextNote.text: Higbee asked what Isaiah meant by telling Zion to put on strength. Verse 8 answers that Isaiah spoke of people called in the last days. They would hold priesthood power “to bring again Zion” and redeem Israel. To put on strength is “to put on the authority of the priesthood.” Verse 10 adds that the scattered must return to the Lord to receive revelation. In this passage, strength is restored authority that Zion had lost and may regain.

passages.title: An apostle is told to prepare for a mission abroad
passages.setting: David W. Patten, a member of the Twelve, was living in Far West, Missouri, by 1837. In April 1838, he reported he could not support several apostles who had turned against Joseph Smith. On 11 April 1838, Joseph dictated this revelation for Patten at Far West. A July 1838 revelation later set the Twelve’s mission abroad for 1839. Patten was killed in October 1838, before that mission began.
passages.summary: The revelation tells David W. Patten to settle his business as soon as he can. He is to dispose of his merchandise. This will free him to go on a mission the next spring. He will go with others, twelve including himself, to testify to all the world. The revelation then says some among them deny the Lord’s name. Others will be planted in their place and receive their “bishopric.”

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 111–114 includes this short revelation to David W. Patten. Why might verse 1 ask Patten to settle his business before serving, and what does verse 2 promise about the quorum?

contextNote.title: Offices pass to those who stay faithful
contextNote.text: Several apostles had turned against Joseph Smith by spring 1838. Verse 1 plans a mission of “twelve including himself,” assuming a full quorum. Verse 2 explains how that will happen if some fall away. Those who “deny my name” will be replaced by others planted in their stead. Here “bishopric” means an office or charge, as in the King James wording of Acts 1:20. In this passage, the calling continues even when particular holders leave it.

passages.title: A named church is told to gather and build at Far West
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Far West, Missouri, on 26 April 1838. He had moved there from Kirtland in March, after dissent divided the Church in Ohio. Thousands of Saints lived in and around Far West, and hundreds more were on the way. Members had begun digging a temple foundation in 1837, but leaders paused the work until the Lord’s will was known. George W. Robinson copied the revelation into Joseph’s journal.
passages.summary: The revelation addresses the First Presidency, Bishop Edward Partridge, the high council in Zion, and all members. It gives the Church its name: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. It calls the Saints to “arise and shine forth” as a standard for the nations. Gathering to Zion and her stakes is to be a defense and a refuge. Far West is declared holy, and a house of worship is to be built there. Work is to begin on 4 July, following a pattern shown to the presidency. Joseph, Sidney Rigdon, and Hyrum Smith must not go further into debt to build it. Far West is to grow quickly, and Joseph will name other stakes nearby.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 115–120 notes that the Lord named His Church in verse 4. How do verses 5–6 describe what the people who bear that name are to do for others?

contextNote.title: A name that carries a duty
contextNote.text: Before 1838 the Church had used other names, including the Church of Christ and the Church of the Latter Day Saints. Verse 4 settles the matter with one name for “the last days.” The name joins two claims: the church belongs to Jesus Christ, and its members are latter-day saints. Verse 3 shows who carries the name, the “elders and people” scattered in all the world. Verse 5 then gives the named people a task, to be “a standard for the nations.” In this passage, the name is an identity that comes with a public duty.

passages.title: A Missouri hill is named as the place Adam will return
passages.setting: In mid-May 1838, Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and others traveled north from Far West into Daviess County, Missouri. On 19 May they went from their camp to Lyman Wight’s ferry on the Grand River to choose land for a new city. Wight had settled near a rise called Spring Hill and urged others to settle there. Joseph’s journal, kept by George W. Robinson, records the new name for the site. The official heading gives the date more loosely as May or June 1838.
passages.summary: This section is one sentence from Joseph Smith’s journal, not a full revelation. It reports that the Lord named Spring Hill “Adam-ondi-Ahman.” It then gives the reason for the name. The place is where Adam “shall come to visit his people.” It links the site to the Ancient of Days in the prophet Daniel’s vision.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 115–120 includes this short entry about Adam-ondi-Ahman. What does verse 1 suggest about why Adam would “visit his people” there, and how does Daniel 7:9–14 help explain it?

contextNote.title: Why a frontier hill got an ancient name
contextNote.text: The Saints needed new places to settle as Far West filled up. Verse 1 explains why this particular hill received a new name. The reason looks ahead: Adam “shall come to visit his people” there. The verse ties that visit to Daniel’s scene of the Ancient of Days sitting in judgment. An earlier revelation, section 107, places a past gathering of Adam’s descendants at Adam-ondi-Ahman. Here the name marks the new settlement as the site of a future meeting as well.

passages.title: Leave Kirtland’s property behind, for property is little to God
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Far West, Missouri, on 8 July 1838. It was one of five he dictated that Sunday about Church leaders and finances. William Marks presided over the Church in Kirtland, Ohio, and handled debts for Joseph and Sidney Rigdon. Newel K. Whitney was the Kirtland bishop. Oliver Granger, a Church agent, had probably just arrived from Kirtland with news.
passages.summary: The revelation tells William Marks and Bishop Whitney to settle their business and leave Kirtland before winter. It warns that delay will not go well for them. It asks them to repent of covetous desires and asks, “what is property unto me?” The Kirtland properties may go to pay debts. The voice points to Adam-ondi-Ahman as land with room enough. Marks is to preside at Far West, and Whitney is to be a bishop at Adam-ondi-Ahman after turning from his “littleness of soul.” Oliver Granger is to work for the First Presidency’s redemption, and his name will be held in sacred remembrance. He is to come to Zion and in time become a merchant for the Lord’s people. Last, the Kirtland members are told to keep the Lord’s house holy.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 115–120 takes its title from verse 13, about Oliver Granger’s sacrifice. What do verses 4–8 say about property, and how do they change the way verse 13 measures success?

contextNote.title: Sacrifice that counts more than gain
contextNote.text: Oliver Granger was sent back to Kirtland to settle the First Presidency’s debts, a hard and uncertain task. Verse 13 tells him to contend for “the redemption of the First Presidency.” It also expects setbacks: “when he falls he shall rise again.” The reason given is that his sacrifice is “more sacred” than his increase. Verse 4 sets up this contrast by asking what property means to God. In this passage, sacrifice means faithful effort valued apart from its financial result.

passages.title: The Twelve are refilled and sent across the sea
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Far West, Missouri, on 8 July 1838. Leaders had prayed to know the Lord’s will about the Twelve. Dissent in 1837 and 1838 had cost the quorum four members. Luke Johnson, John Boynton, and Lyman Johnson were cut off, and William McLellin was found in transgression. Thomas Marsh, the quorum president, was the only apostle at the meeting.
passages.summary: The revelation calls for a conference to organize the Twelve and fill the places of the fallen. It tells Thomas to stay in Zion for a time to publish the word. The other apostles are to keep preaching with humility and patience. If they do, the Lord promises to provide for their families. Next spring they are to cross “the great waters” to preach. They are to leave from the Far West temple site on 26 April 1839. John Taylor, John Page, Wilford Woodruff, and Willard Richards are named to fill the vacancies.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 115–120 covers this call to the Twelve. What promise does verse 3 attach to serving “in all lowliness of heart,” and who receives it?

contextNote.title: A departure fixed to a date and a place
contextNote.text: The quorum had lost members and needed both new apostles and a mission. Verse 5 sets an exact date and place for leaving: 26 April 1839, at the Far West temple site. Verse 4 gives the purpose, to preach the gospel over the great waters. By that spring the Saints had been driven from Missouri, and Far West was hostile ground. Wilford Woodruff’s journal records a meeting at the site that day, where new apostles were ordained. In this passage, the date ties the mission’s start to the place where the temple was to stand.

passages.title: Tithing begins with surplus, then a tenth of yearly increase
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Far West, Missouri, on 8 July 1838. He had asked how much of the Saints’ property the Lord required as tithing. At that time “tithing” meant any donation to Church funds, not a set tenth. The Church carried heavy debt from the Kirtland Temple, failed Ohio ventures, and the Panic of 1837. The Saints also needed money to build up their Missouri settlements.
passages.summary: The revelation asks the Saints to give all their surplus property to the bishop in Zion. The funds are for the temple, the foundation of Zion, the priesthood, and the Presidency’s debts. This first gift is called “the beginning of the tithing.” After that, members are to pay one-tenth of their interest each year. The revelation calls this “a standing law” forever. Those who gather to Zion must keep it, or they will not be worthy to stay. If the people do not keep it, the land will not be Zion to them. The law is to be an example for all the stakes.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 115–120 discusses this law of tithing. According to verses 6–7, what does keeping this law do for the land of Zion and its stakes?

contextNote.title: One-tenth of interest, after the surplus
contextNote.text: Joseph Smith asked how much property the Lord required, and verses 1–4 answer in two steps. First, verse 1 asks for all surplus property, given once to the bishop. Then verse 4 sets an ongoing rule of “one-tenth of all their interest annually.” A Joseph Smith Papers note explains surplus as property the owner could not put to good use. Church leaders have long read “interest” as a person’s yearly increase or income. In this passage, tithing is a yearly tenth of increase built on an earlier one-time gift.

passages.title: Tithed funds are to be handled by a council, not one leader
passages.setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Far West, Missouri, on 8 July 1838. It followed section 119 on the same day and answered how tithed property should be used. In 1837 two Missouri leaders had made money decisions without the bishop or high council. That had caused resentment among high council members. The council named here met as directed on 26 July 1838.
passages.summary: This short revelation follows directly from the law of tithing in section 119. It says the time has come to decide how tithed property is used. A council is to make those decisions. The council includes the First Presidency, the bishop and his counselors, and the high council. The revelation adds that the Lord’s “own voice” will guide them.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 115–120 pairs this verse with the law of tithing. Why might verse 1 require both a council and the Lord’s “own voice” for these decisions?

contextNote.title: Shared decisions over shared money
contextNote.text: Leaders in Missouri had disputed who could spend Church funds. Verse 1 answers by naming three bodies who decide together. They are the First Presidency, the bishop and his council, and the high council. No single leader controls the tithes under this plan. The verse also adds a further voice: decisions come “by mine own voice unto them.” In this passage, a council means joint judgment that still seeks revelation.

passages.title: A prisoner’s cry is answered with peace and limits on priesthood power
passages.setting: Joseph Smith wrote this from the jail at Liberty, Clay County, Missouri, in March 1839. He, Hyrum Smith, Lyman Wight, Caleb Baldwin, and Alexander McRae had been held there since 1 December 1838. They awaited trial on charges from the 1838 conflict in Missouri. Governor Lilburn Boggs had ordered the Saints out of the state, and most had fled to Illinois. Appeals to officials had brought no relief. The section joins passages from two letters to Bishop Edward Partridge and the Church, dated 20 March and about 22 March.
passages.summary: The section opens with a prayer: “O God, where art thou?” Joseph asks how long the Saints must suffer and pleads for God to act. A reply then speaks to him as “my son” and promises peace. His trial will be “but a small moment,” and his friends still stand by him. The text warns those who falsely accuse the Saints, drive them, and kill them. It promises knowledge by the Holy Ghost that has not been revealed before. It says many are called but few chosen, because they seek worldly honors. Priesthood power, it says, rests only on persuasion, patience, gentleness, meekness, kindness, and unfeigned love.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 121–123 takes its title from verse 1. It links Joseph’s prayer in verses 1–6 to the answer of peace in verses 7–8. Which qualities in verses 41–45 describe how you could use any influence you hold at home or at church?

contextNote.title: Why priesthood cannot be forced
contextNote.text: Verse 39 states the problem: people who get “a little authority” soon practice “unrighteous dominion.” Verse 36 explains why that fails, because priesthood rights are tied to “the powers of heaven.” Verse 37 adds that when someone uses compulsion, “the heavens withdraw themselves.” Verse 41 then lists the only means that keep priesthood influence: persuasion, long-suffering, gentleness, meekness, and unfeigned love. Joseph wrote this while he himself was held by force. In this passage, power means influence earned by love, not control taken by pressure.

passages.title: Suffering can teach, because Christ descended below it all
passages.setting: Joseph Smith was a prisoner in the jail at Liberty, Missouri, when this text was written. It comes from a letter to Bishop Edward Partridge and the Church dated about 22 March 1839. Joseph likely dictated it, and fellow prisoner Alexander McRae wrote it out. In the letter the voice shifts from the prisoners to words addressed to Joseph as “my son.” By then Joseph had been held in Liberty for nearly four months.
passages.summary: The voice tells Joseph that the ends of the earth will ask about his name. Fools will mock him, but the pure in heart will seek his counsel. Traitors will not turn his people against him. It then lists trials: false accusation, being torn from family, prison, and a sentence of death. It pictures his six-year-old son clinging to him and asking why he cannot stay. All these things, it says, “shall give thee experience” and be for his good. It says the Son of Man has descended below them all. Joseph should hold on, for his days are known and God will be with him.

lds.text: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 121–123 teaches that the Savior understands every trial. How does the question in verse 8 change the meaning of the hardships listed in verses 5–7?

contextNote.title: Measured against Christ’s descent
contextNote.text: Verses 5–7 list hardship after hardship that could fall on Joseph, up to “the very jaws of hell.” It claims all of them can give experience and work for his good. Verse 8 gives the reason in a short question: “Art thou greater than he?” The Son of Man, it says, “hath descended below them all.” Joseph’s suffering is placed beneath Christ’s, not outside God’s knowledge. Verse 9 then draws the result: hold on, because the enemies’ bounds and Joseph’s days are set. In this passage, descending means taking on suffering deeper than any Joseph faced.

passages.title: Record the wrongs, then stand still to see God’s salvation
passages.setting: Joseph Smith wrote this in the jail at Liberty, Missouri, in an undated letter of about 22 March 1839. His fellow prisoners also signed it. The letter went to Bishop Edward Partridge and the Church, by way of Quincy, Illinois, where many Saints had fled. The Saints had lost homes, land, and lives in the Missouri conflict of 1838. The letter recalls the killings at Hawn’s Mill and the death of apostle David Patten.
passages.summary: The letter suggests the Saints gather the facts of their suffering in Missouri. They should record property losses and injuries to character and person.
