campaigns.title: Joseph and Oliver move from Harmony to Fayette
campaigns.summary: Opposition near Harmony led David Whitmer to bring Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery to his father's farm at Fayette. Translation was finished there in June 1829.

campaigns.title: Mission to the Lamanites
stops: Wyandot lands near Upper Sandusky, Ohio
campaigns.summary: Oliver Cowdery, Parley P. Pratt, Peter Whitmer Jr., and Ziba Peterson left New York in October 1830. They stopped near Kirtland, visited the Wyandot in Ohio, and reached the Missouri border in January 1831.
campaigns.detail: Stops: Fayette → Buffalo, New York → Kirtland → Wyandot lands near Upper Sandusky, Ohio → Independence → Lands west of Missouri.
campaigns.evidence: Main stops of the mission; the line between them is simplified
campaigns.uncertainty: Main stops of the mission; the line between them is simplified

campaigns.title: The New York Saints gather to Ohio
campaigns.summary: Sections 37 and 38 command the New York members to gather to Ohio. Joseph and Emma Smith arrived in Kirtland about 1 February 1831; most branches followed by May, many by way of Buffalo and Lake Erie.
campaigns.detail: Stops: Fayette → Buffalo, New York → Kirtland.
campaigns.evidence: Commanded move; common route by the Erie Canal and Lake Erie
campaigns.uncertainty: Commanded move; common route by the Erie Canal and Lake Erie

campaigns.title: The Colesville Branch moves to Thompson, then Missouri
campaigns.summary: The Colesville Saints settled at Thompson, Ohio, in May 1831. When the land arrangement there failed, section 54 sent them on to Missouri. They arrived in Jackson County in late July 1831.
campaigns.detail: Stops: Colesville → Buffalo, New York → Thompson → Cincinnati → St. Louis → Independence.

campaigns.title: Elders travel to Missouri, summer 1831
campaigns.summary: Section 52 sent elders in pairs to Missouri. Joseph Smith's party went by canal and river to St. Louis, then walked west to Independence in July 1831.
campaigns.detail: Stops: Kirtland → Cincinnati → Louisville, Kentucky → St. Louis → Independence.
campaigns.evidence: Joseph Smith's party; other pairs took different roads
campaigns.uncertainty: Joseph Smith's party; other pairs took different roads

campaigns.title: Return journey down the Missouri River
campaigns.summary: In August 1831 Joseph Smith and ten elders started home by canoe on the Missouri River. After danger at McIlwaine's Bend (section 61), most went on by land. They met other elders at Chariton (section 62) and reached Kirtland late in August.
campaigns.detail: Stops: Independence → McIlwaine’s Bend → Chariton → St. Louis → Cincinnati → Kirtland.
campaigns.evidence: Places named in sections 60–62; later legs simplified
campaigns.uncertainty: Places named in sections 60–62; later legs simplified

campaigns.title: Joseph Smith visits Missouri, spring 1832
campaigns.summary: Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Newel K. Whitney traveled to Independence in April 1832 to organize the Church's business and care for the poor (sections 78, 82, 83).
campaigns.detail: Stops: Hiram → Louisville, Kentucky → St. Louis → Independence.

campaigns.title: Mission to Upper Canada
campaigns.summary: Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon left Kirtland in October 1833. Section 100 came at Perrysburg, New York; they then preached at Mount Pleasant, Upper Canada.

campaigns.title: Saints driven from Jackson County
campaigns.summary: In November 1833 armed residents drove about 1,200 Latter-day Saints from Jackson County. Most crossed the Missouri River north into Clay County.
campaigns.evidence: Forced move; Liberty stands for Clay County
campaigns.uncertainty: Forced move; Liberty stands for Clay County

campaigns.title: Camp of Israel (Zion's Camp)
campaigns.summary: Section 103 called for men to go to Zion's aid. About 200 volunteers marched from Ohio in May 1834. Section 105 came at Fishing River in June and told them not to fight; the camp disbanded soon after.
campaigns.detail: Stops: Kirtland → New Portage, Ohio → Indianapolis, Indiana → Jacksonville, Illinois → Louisiana, Missouri → Salt River settlement, Missouri → Fishing River.
campaigns.evidence: Representative towns on the march; route simplified
campaigns.uncertainty: Representative towns on the march; route simplified

campaigns.title: Journey to Salem, Massachusetts
campaigns.summary: Joseph Smith, Hyrum Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Oliver Cowdery traveled east in summer 1836, partly hoping to raise money for Church debts. Section 111 came at Salem in August.
campaigns.detail: Stops: Kirtland → Buffalo, New York → Albany, New York → New York City → Salem.

campaigns.title: Joseph Smith moves from Kirtland to Far West
campaigns.summary: Joseph Smith left Kirtland in January 1838 amid dissent and lawsuits. He arrived in Far West, Missouri, in March 1838.

campaigns.title: Joseph Smith taken to Liberty Jail
campaigns.summary: After the Saints surrendered at Far West in November 1838, Joseph Smith and other leaders were held at Independence and Richmond. In December they were sent to the jail at Liberty.
campaigns.detail: Stops: Far West → Independence → Richmond, Missouri → Liberty.

campaigns.title: Saints leave Missouri for Illinois
campaigns.summary: Under Governor Boggs's expulsion order, thousands of Saints left Missouri in the winter of 1838–39. Many found refuge at Quincy, Illinois, then settled at Commerce, later Nauvoo.
campaigns.evidence: Main refuge and settlement; families took many roads
campaigns.uncertainty: Main refuge and settlement; families took many roads

campaigns.title: Joseph and Hyrum Smith go to Carthage
campaigns.summary: Joseph and Hyrum Smith went to Carthage in June 1844 to answer charges and were held in the county jail. A mob killed them there on 27 June 1844.

campaigns.title: Across Iowa to Winter Quarters
campaigns.summary: The Saints began leaving Nauvoo in February 1846 under threat of violence. They crossed Iowa, set up way stations, and wintered on the Missouri River.
campaigns.detail: Stops: Nauvoo → Sugar Creek camp, Iowa Territory → Garden Grove, Iowa → Mount Pisgah, Iowa → Council Bluffs (Kanesville), Iowa → Winter Quarters.

campaigns.title: The vanguard company goes west
campaigns.summary: Section 136 organized the companies for the trek. Brigham Young's vanguard company left in April 1847 and reached the Salt Lake Valley in July.
campaigns.detail: Stops: Winter Quarters → Fort Laramie → South Pass → Fort Bridger → Salt Lake City.

regions.name: New York
regions.detail: Joseph Smith’s family farmed near Palmyra, and the Church was organized at Fayette in 1830.

regions.name: Pennsylvania
regions.detail: Joseph and Emma Smith lived at Harmony, on the Susquehanna River, while most of the Book of Mormon was translated.

regions.name: Ohio
regions.detail: Kirtland was Church headquarters from 1831 to 1838. Revelations call the region “the Ohio.”

regions.name: Missouri
regions.summary: A U.S. state since 1821; the western edge of the nation in the 1830s.
regions.detail: Revelations named Jackson County as Zion in 1831. Saints were driven from the county in 1833 and from the state in 1838–39.

regions.name: Illinois
regions.detail: Quincy sheltered refugees from Missouri, and Nauvoo became headquarters from 1839 to 1846.

regions.name: Massachusetts
regions.detail: Section 111 was received at Salem in 1836.

regions.name: Iowa Territory
regions.summary: Organized as a U.S. territory in July 1838; a state from December 1846.
regions.detail: Saints settled across the river from Nauvoo, and in 1846 they crossed it toward the Missouri River.

regions.name: Michigan
regions.summary: A U.S. territory until 1837, then a state.
regions.detail: Section 52 sends missionaries by way of Detroit.

regions.name: Lands west of Missouri
regions.summary: Unorganized land outside any state, set aside in the 1830s for Native nations moved from the East.
regions.detail: The 1830–31 mission to the Lamanites reached the Delaware nation just west of Independence.

regions.name: Lands west of the Missouri River
regions.summary: Unorganized land outside any state in the 1840s.
regions.detail: Winter Quarters stood here in 1846–48, on land of the Omaha nation.

regions.name: Upper Canada
regions.summary: A British colony; part of the Province of Canada from 1841.
regions.detail: Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon preached at Mount Pleasant in 1833 (section 100).

regions.name: Mexico (northern frontier)
regions.summary: Part of Mexico until the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in February 1848.
regions.detail: The Salt Lake Valley lay inside Mexico when the pioneers arrived in July 1847.

words.label: Zion
words.meaning: Zion is the name the revelations give to a holy city and a holy people. It can mean a place, a gathered community, or the pure in heart.
words.discussion: Early revelations tell workers to “seek to bring forth and establish the cause of Zion” (D&C 6:6). D&C 57:1–3 names Independence, Missouri, as the center place for the city. Later sections speak of Zion’s redemption after the Saints were driven out (D&C 101; 105). D&C 97:21 defines Zion as “the pure in heart.”

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Zion

words.label: Stake
words.meaning: A stake is a regional church unit that supports Zion. The word comes from the tent stakes that hold up a tent.
words.discussion: D&C 82:13–14 calls Kirtland “a stake to Zion” and says Zion’s stakes must be strengthened. D&C 101:21 says new gathering places “shall be called stakes, for the curtains or the strength of Zion.” By D&C 124 a stake at Nauvoo has its own president and high council.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Stake

words.label: Bishop
words.meaning: A bishop is a church officer who cares for the poor and manages church property. The bishopric is the office or the group that holds it.
words.discussion: Edward Partridge is called as the first bishop in D&C 41:9. Under D&C 42:30–34 members consecrate property before the bishop, who keeps the surplus for the needy. D&C 107:68–72 says the bishop administers “temporal things” and acts as “a judge in Israel.”

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Bishop

words.label: Elder
words.meaning: An elder is an office in the Melchizedek Priesthood. In the D&C the elders are the main traveling preachers and local leaders.
words.discussion: D&C 20:38–45 lists an elder’s duties: to baptize, ordain, give the Holy Ghost, and lead meetings. It also says “an apostle is an elder.” Many revelations send pairs of elders to preach, as in D&C 52. D&C 107:7 places the office under the Melchizedek Priesthood.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Elder

words.label: High priest
words.meaning: A high priest is an office in the Melchizedek Priesthood. High priests could preside, serve as bishops, and sit on high councils.
words.discussion: The first high priests in the restored church were ordained in June 1831. D&C 68:15–19 says bishops are to be chosen from worthy high priests. D&C 102:1 forms a high council of twelve high priests. D&C 107:53 also calls Adam’s righteous descendants high priests.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: High Priest

words.label: Priest
words.meaning: In the D&C a priest is usually an office in the Aaronic Priesthood. Priests may baptize and administer the sacrament.
words.discussion: D&C 20:46–52 lists a priest’s duties: to preach, baptize, administer the sacrament, and visit members’ homes. D&C 107:87 sets a president over forty-eight priests. The word also appears in other senses, such as “kings and priests” in D&C 76:56. In “high priest” it names a different office.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Priest, Aaronic Priesthood

words.label: Teacher
words.meaning: A teacher is an office in the Aaronic Priesthood. Teachers watch over church members and strengthen them.
words.discussion: D&C 20:53–59 says the teacher must “watch over the church always” and prevent strife among members. Teachers may not baptize or administer the sacrament (D&C 20:58). D&C 84:111 calls teachers and deacons “standing ministers” for local members. In D&C 88:128 “teacher” instead means the presiding instructor of the school of the prophets.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Teacher, Aaronic Priesthood

words.label: Deacon
words.meaning: A deacon is the first office in the Aaronic Priesthood. Deacons assist teachers and other officers.
words.discussion: D&C 20:57–59 says deacons assist teachers and may warn, exhort, and teach. They may not baptize or administer the sacrament. D&C 107:85 sets a president over twelve deacons.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Deacon

words.label: Aaronic Priesthood
words.meaning: The Aaronic Priesthood is the lesser of the two priesthoods named in the D&C. It is named after Aaron, the brother of Moses.
words.discussion: D&C 13 records the words Joseph Smith reported John the Baptist spoke when conferring the “Priesthood of Aaron” in 1829. D&C 107:13–14 explains the name and calls it the lesser priesthood. D&C 107:20 says it holds “the keys of the ministering of angels” and outward ordinances such as baptism.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Aaronic Priesthood

words.label: Melchizedek Priesthood
words.meaning: The Melchizedek Priesthood is the higher of the two priesthoods named in the D&C. The revelations also call it the High Priesthood.
words.discussion: D&C 107:2–4 says it is named after Melchizedek, an ancient high priest, to avoid overusing God’s name. D&C 107:18–19 says it holds the keys of “all the spiritual blessings of the church.” D&C 84:6–17 traces a line of this priesthood back through Moses to Adam.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Melchizedek Priesthood

words.label: Keys
words.meaning: In the D&C “keys” means the right to lead and direct a work of God. It is about authority, not physical keys.
words.discussion: D&C 13:1 says the Aaronic Priesthood holds “the keys of the ministering of angels.” In D&C 110:11–16 Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery reported that Moses, Elias, and Elijah gave them keys. D&C 81:2 says the keys of the kingdom belong to the Presidency of the High Priesthood.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Keys of the Priesthood

words.label: Consecration
words.meaning: To consecrate is to dedicate something to God. In the D&C it often means giving property to the church for the poor and for building Zion.
words.discussion: D&C 42:30–34 tells members to consecrate their property before the bishop “with a covenant and a deed.” Each member then received a stewardship, and the surplus went to the storehouse. The word is also used more broadly, for a consecrated land or house (D&C 57:1; 109:12).

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Consecrate, Law of Consecration
Church History Topics: Consecration and Stewardship

words.label: Stewardship
words.meaning: A steward manages what belongs to someone else. In the D&C a stewardship is a portion of property or duty that a person must account for.
words.discussion: D&C 42:32 makes each member “a steward over his own property” after consecration. D&C 72:3 says every steward must render an account. D&C 104:11–13 divides the united firm’s property into stewardships and says God makes “every man accountable, as a steward over earthly blessings.”

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Steward, Stewardship
Church History Topics: Consecration and Stewardship

words.label: Storehouse
words.meaning: The storehouse held goods and funds that the bishop used to care for the poor.
words.discussion: D&C 42:34 says the surplus from consecration “shall be kept in my storehouse” for the poor and needy. D&C 72:10 makes keeping the storehouse part of a bishop’s work. D&C 83:5–6 says widows and orphans have a claim on the storehouse.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Storehouse

words.label: Tithing
words.meaning: Tithing means giving a tenth. In D&C 119 it means surplus property first, then one-tenth of yearly “interest.”
words.discussion: D&C 64:23 calls the present “a day for the tithing of my people.” D&C 119:1–4, given in 1838, asks for surplus property and then one-tenth of interest annually. D&C 120 then names a council to decide how tithing is spent.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Tithes, Tithing
Church History Topics: Tithing

words.label: Endowment
words.meaning: To be endowed is to be given a gift. In the D&C the endowment is a promised gift of “power from on high.”
words.discussion: D&C 38:32 tells the Saints to go to Ohio, where they would “be endowed with power from on high.” D&C 95:8 and 105:33 tie this promise to the house of the Lord in Kirtland. D&C 110:9 links the endowment to that temple’s dedication in 1836.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Endowment

words.label: Sealing
words.meaning: To seal is to bind or confirm with authority. In the D&C sealing power binds something on earth so it is also bound in heaven.
words.discussion: D&C 128:8–9 describes power by which “whatsoever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven.” D&C 124:124 gives Hyrum Smith “the sealing blessings” of the church. D&C 132 applies sealing to marriage. The word “sealed” is not linked, because it often has other meanings, such as a sealed book.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Seal, Sealing

words.label: Celestial
words.meaning: Celestial means heavenly. In the D&C it names the highest of three kingdoms of glory after the resurrection.
words.discussion: In D&C 76:50–70 Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon reported seeing those who inherit celestial glory, compared to the sun. D&C 88:22 says one must abide a celestial law to receive a celestial glory. D&C 131:1 says the celestial glory has three heavens or degrees.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Celestial Glory

words.label: Terrestrial
words.meaning: Terrestrial means earthly. In the D&C it names the middle of three kingdoms of glory.
words.discussion: D&C 76:71–80 describes the terrestrial world, whose glory is compared to the moon. Verse 79 says its people were “not valiant in the testimony of Jesus.” D&C 88:23 ties terrestrial glory to a terrestrial law.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Terrestrial Glory

words.label: Telestial
words.meaning: Telestial is a word coined in the D&C. It names the lowest of three kingdoms of glory.
words.discussion: D&C 76:81–112 describes telestial glory, compared to the stars. Verse 82 says its people “received not the gospel of Christ.” D&C 88:24 says those who cannot abide even a telestial law inherit no kingdom of glory.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Telestial Glory

words.label: Urim and Thummim
words.meaning: The Urim and Thummim was an instrument for receiving revelation. Joseph Smith said he used it to translate the Book of Mormon.
words.discussion: D&C 10:1 says Joseph translated “by the means of the Urim and Thummim.” D&C 17:1 promises the Three Witnesses a view of it along with the plates. D&C 130:8–10 extends the idea, calling the place where God resides “a great Urim and Thummim.”

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Urim and Thummim
Church History Topics: Seer Stones

words.label: Seer
words.meaning: A seer is a person who sees what others cannot, by God’s power. The D&C uses the title for the church president.
words.discussion: D&C 21:1 says Joseph Smith shall be called “a seer, a translator, a prophet.” D&C 107:92 says the president of the High Priesthood is to be a seer and revelator. D&C 124:94 extends the title to Hyrum Smith.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Seer

words.label: Lamanites
words.meaning: The Lamanites are a people in the Book of Mormon. Early church members applied the name to Native Americans.
words.discussion: D&C 3:18–20 says the Book of Mormon was preserved so the Lamanites could know the promises of the Lord. D&C 28:8 and 32:2 send Oliver Cowdery and others on a mission to the Lamanites in 1830. That mission led west to Missouri, near the later site of Zion.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Lamanites

words.label: Gathering
words.meaning: The gathering means bringing believers together into one place or people. The D&C links it to the ancient promise to gather Israel.
words.discussion: D&C 29:7–8 calls the elders to bring about “the gathering of mine elect” to one place. D&C 57:1 names Missouri as the land “for the gathering of the saints.” In D&C 110:11 Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery reported receiving “the keys of the gathering of Israel” from Moses.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Gathering of Israel

words.label: School of the Prophets
words.meaning: The school of the prophets was a class for church leaders in Kirtland, Ohio. It began in early 1833.
words.discussion: D&C 88:127–141 sets rules for the school, including how members greet one another. D&C 90:7 gives its keys to the First Presidency. D&C 95:10 rebukes contention that arose in the school. The Word of Wisdom (D&C 89) was first given to the school’s members.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: School of the Prophets
Church History Topics: School of the Prophets

words.label: Word of Wisdom
words.meaning: The Word of Wisdom is the title of D&C 89, a revelation about food, drink, and health.
words.discussion: D&C 89 was given in February 1833 for the high priests meeting in Kirtland. Verse 2 says it came “not by commandment or constraint.” It advises against wine, strong drink, tobacco, and hot drinks, and praises grain and fruit. Verses 18–21 promise health and wisdom to those who keep it. In D&C 46:17 “word of wisdom” means a spiritual gift instead, so only the title in D&C 89:1 is linked.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Word of Wisdom

words.label: Conference
words.meaning: A conference was a meeting of church members and officers to do church business.
words.discussion: D&C 20:61–62 tells the elders to meet in conference every three months. D&C 28:10 says Joseph Smith would preside at a coming conference in Fayette. D&C 73:2 and other revelations send elders out “by the voice of the conference.”

words.label: High council
words.meaning: A high council is a body of twelve high priests who help govern the church and judge serious disputes.
words.discussion: D&C 102 records the organization of the first high council in Kirtland in February 1834. Verse 2 says it was formed to settle difficulties that local councils could not. D&C 107:33 calls the Twelve a “Traveling Presiding High Council.”

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: High Council

words.label: First Presidency
words.meaning: The First Presidency is the church’s highest governing council. It is made up of the president and his counselors.
words.discussion: D&C 81:2 and 90:6 describe Joseph Smith and his counselors as holding the keys of the kingdom. D&C 107:22 says three presiding high priests form the quorum of the presidency. D&C 120:1 includes the First Presidency in the council over tithing funds.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: First Presidency

words.label: The Twelve (Quorum of the Twelve Apostles)
words.meaning: The Twelve are twelve apostles called as special witnesses of Christ. They form a quorum that travels to lead the church abroad.
words.discussion: D&C 18:27–37, given in 1829, tells Oliver Cowdery and David Whitmer to seek out the Twelve. The first quorum was chosen in 1835. D&C 107:23–24 says the Twelve are “special witnesses” equal in authority to the First Presidency. D&C 112 instructs Thomas B. Marsh and the Twelve.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Apostle

words.label: Seventy
words.meaning: The Seventy are a priesthood office of traveling preachers. They are organized in groups of seventy men.
words.discussion: D&C 107:25–26 calls the Seventy “especial witnesses unto the Gentiles” and forms them into a quorum. D&C 107:93–97 says seven presidents preside over them. D&C 124:138 names presidents over “the quorum of seventies.” Lowercase “seventy” is not linked because D&C 98:40 uses it as a number.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Seventy

words.label: Patriarch
words.meaning: A patriarch is a father figure who gives blessings. In the D&C a church patriarch gives patriarchal blessings to members.
words.discussion: D&C 124:91–92 gives Hyrum Smith the office of patriarch, held earlier by his father, Joseph Smith Sr. Hyrum was to “hold the keys of the patriarchal blessings” of the church. D&C 135:1 calls him “Hyrum Smith the Patriarch.”

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Patriarch, Patriarchal
Church History Topics: Patriarchal Blessings

words.label: Ordinance
words.meaning: An ordinance is a sacred rite done with authority, such as baptism. It can also mean a rule or law.
words.discussion: D&C 1:15 accuses people of having “strayed from mine ordinances.” D&C 84:20–21 says the power of godliness is shown in the ordinances of the priesthood. D&C 124 and 128 apply the word to temple rites, including baptism for the dead.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Ordinances

words.label: Baptism for the dead
words.meaning: Baptism for the dead is a baptism a living person receives on behalf of someone who has died.
words.discussion: Joseph Smith began teaching the practice in Nauvoo in 1840. D&C 124:29–33 says it belongs in a temple and commands the Saints to build one. D&C 127 and 128 are letters requiring a recorder to witness each baptism. D&C 128:18 says the living and the dead cannot be made perfect without each other.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Salvation for the Dead
Church History Topics: Baptism for the Dead

words.label: Adam-ondi-Ahman
words.meaning: Adam-ondi-Ahman is a name from the D&C. It names the land where Adam lived and a settlement in Daviess County, Missouri.
words.discussion: D&C 107:53–56 says Adam gathered his righteous descendants in “the valley of Adam-ondi-Ahman” to bless them. D&C 116:1, from 1838, says Spring Hill, Missouri, was named Adam-ondi-Ahman. That verse says it is where Adam “shall come to visit his people.”

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Adam-ondi-Ahman

words.label: The Ohio
words.meaning: “The Ohio” was an early name for the state of Ohio and its region. Kirtland, Ohio, became church headquarters in 1831.
words.discussion: D&C 37:1–3 tells the church in New York to “assemble together at the Ohio.” D&C 38:32 promises that in Ohio the Saints would receive God’s law and be “endowed with power.” D&C 39:15 promises a blessing to those who gather there.

related.label: Church History Topics: Kirtland, Ohio

words.label: Gentiles
words.meaning: In the Bible, Gentiles are people who are not Israelites. Early church members often counted themselves among the Gentiles.
words.discussion: D&C 45:28–30 speaks of “the times of the Gentiles” and the gospel coming to them. D&C 107:25 and 107:97 send the Seventy to the Gentiles first, then to the Jews. In D&C 109:60 Joseph Smith’s dedicatory prayer describes the Saints as “identified with the Gentiles.”

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Gentiles

words.label: Sons of perdition
words.meaning: Perdition means loss or ruin. The D&C uses “sons of perdition” for those who deny God after knowing his power.
words.discussion: D&C 76:25–26 says Lucifer was called Perdition after his fall. D&C 76:31–35 describes those who knew God’s power and then denied it. Verses 43–44 say all others are saved except these “sons of perdition.”

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Sons of Perdition
Guide to the Scriptures: Perdition

words.label: Spirit world
words.meaning: The spirit world is the place where the spirits of the dead wait for the resurrection.
words.discussion: D&C 138 records a vision Joseph F. Smith reported in 1918. In verses 18–23 he saw Christ visit the righteous dead. Verses 28–37 say Christ organized messengers to teach “the spirits in prison.” Verse 57 says faithful elders keep preaching there after death.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Spirit World

words.label: New and everlasting covenant
words.meaning: The new and everlasting covenant means the fulness of the gospel and its covenants. In D&C 131 and 132 it refers especially to eternal marriage.
words.discussion: D&C 131:1–4 says entering this order of the priesthood is needed for the highest degree of celestial glory. D&C 132:6–7 says the covenant was instituted for the fulness of God’s glory. D&C 132:19 joins it to marriages sealed by the Holy Spirit of promise. The same section also gave the revelation on plural marriage.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: New and Everlasting Covenant

words.label: Comforter
words.meaning: The Comforter is a title for the Holy Ghost, taken from the Gospel of John.
words.discussion: D&C 36:2 promises that Edward Partridge will receive “the Holy Ghost, even the Comforter.” D&C 42:17 says the Comforter “knoweth all things.” D&C 88:3–4 speaks of “another Comforter,” called the Holy Spirit of promise.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Comforter

words.label: Holy Spirit of promise
words.meaning: The Holy Spirit of promise is the Holy Ghost acting to confirm covenants and blessings as valid.
words.discussion: D&C 76:53 says those in celestial glory are “sealed by the Holy Spirit of promise.” D&C 132:7 says covenants not sealed in this way end at death. D&C 88:3–4 links this Spirit to the promise of eternal life.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Holy Spirit of Promise

words.label: Book of Commandments
words.meaning: The Book of Commandments was the first planned book of Joseph Smith’s revelations. Its printing in Missouri stopped in 1833.
words.discussion: Church leaders agreed to publish the revelations at a November 1831 conference. D&C 1 was given as the preface to that book. In D&C 67:6 the revelation challenges critics to write something like “the least” of its revelations. A mob destroyed the press in Independence in July 1833 before the book was finished.

related.label: Church History Topics: Book of Commandments

words.label: Doctrine and Covenants
words.meaning: The Doctrine and Covenants is a book of Joseph Smith’s revelations and later additions. It was first published in Kirtland in 1835.
words.discussion: D&C 124:141 already refers to “the book of Doctrine and Covenants” for instructions on the bishopric. D&C 135:3 and 135:6 list it among the works Joseph Smith brought forth. Later editions added sections, such as D&C 138 in 1981.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: Doctrine and Covenants

words.label: New Jerusalem
words.meaning: The New Jerusalem is a holy city to be built in the last days. The D&C places it in America and links it with Zion.
words.discussion: D&C 42:9 promises the city will be revealed in time. D&C 45:66–67 calls it “a land of peace, a city of refuge,” and says it will be called Zion. D&C 84:2–4 says the city and its temple will be built in western Missouri.

related.label: Guide to the Scriptures: New Jerusalem

guides.title: Translating the Book of Mormon
guides.description: Follow the revelations that guided the Book of Mormon from the lost pages of 1828 to the printer in 1829.

steps.title: The lost pages are blamed on men, not God
steps.text: In June 1828 Martin Harris lost the first 116 pages of the translation. Joseph Smith received this revelation at Harmony, Pennsylvania, in July, after he learned of the loss. Verse 3 says it is the work of men that is frustrated, not the work of God. Verses 9–10 tell Joseph he is still chosen if he repents. Verse 11 warns that without repentance he will have no more gift. The tour starts here because every later step builds on this setback.

steps.title: Martin Harris is promised three witnesses
steps.text: By March 1829 opposition was growing around Palmyra, and Harris came to Harmony seeking proof. The revelation does not let Joseph show him the plates. Instead, verse 11 promises three servants to whom the plates will be shown. Verse 24 says Harris may see them, but only if he humbles himself in mighty prayer. The same man who lost the pages is offered a new role. That promise waits until step six to be fulfilled.

steps.title: Oliver Cowdery is told how revelation will come
steps.text: In April 1829 Oliver Cowdery arrived in Harmony and began writing as Joseph dictated. With a steady scribe, the translation moved quickly. Oliver wanted a gift to translate as well, and this revelation answered him. Verse 2 promises the Lord will speak to his mind and heart by the Holy Ghost. Verse 3 calls this “the spirit of revelation.” The next revelation explains what happened when Oliver tried.

steps.title: Oliver’s attempt fails, and the method is explained
steps.text: Oliver tried to translate and did not succeed. Verse 7 says he assumed the gift would come if he only asked. Verse 8 says he must first study it out in his mind, then ask if it is right. A burning in the bosom would confirm it, and a stupor of thought would not. Verse 10 says it is not expedient for him to translate now, so he should keep writing. The promise of section 8 now came with a condition Oliver had missed.

steps.title: The lost pages will not be translated again
steps.text: Near the end of the work, Joseph and Oliver faced the old problem of the 116 pages. The date of this revelation is uncertain; the official heading favors April 1829, with parts possibly from 1828. It says the men holding the pages had altered them to discredit a second translation. Verses 41–42 tell Joseph to translate the fuller account on the plates of Nephi instead. Verse 43 says the Lord will not let them destroy his work. This answers the loss described in step one.

steps.title: Three witnesses are told what they will see
steps.text: Joseph finished translating at the Whitmer home in Fayette, New York, in June 1829. Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer, and Martin Harris each wanted to be a witness. Verse 1 lists what they would see, including the plates and the Urim and Thummim. Verse 5 says they will testify that they have seen them as Joseph has seen them. Joseph later said the four men soon went into the woods to pray for the promised view. The promise first given to Harris in section 5 was now tied to a time and place.

steps.title: Martin Harris is told to pay for the printing
steps.text: A finished manuscript still needed a printer. Egbert Grandin of Palmyra asked $3,000 for five thousand copies. Verse 26 tells Harris not to covet his own property but to pay for the printing. Verse 35 adds, “Pay the debt thou hast contracted with the printer.” On 25 August 1829 Harris mortgaged his farm to Grandin. The Book of Mormon went on sale in March 1830. The man whose loss opened this tour paid for its completion.

guides.title: Organizing the Church
guides.description: Trace how the Church gained leaders, rules, and councils from its first meeting in 1830 to the priesthood instruction of 1835.

steps.title: The new church is told to heed Joseph’s word
steps.text: On 6 April 1830 a small group met at Peter Whitmer Sr.’s home in Fayette, New York. They voted to accept Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery as teachers, and the two ordained each other elders. Joseph dictated this revelation while the group was still together. Verse 1 says a record must be kept naming Joseph a seer, translator, prophet, apostle, and elder. Verse 5 tells the Church to receive his word “as if from mine own mouth.” From its first day, the Church was organized around this claim of revelation.

steps.title: The Articles and Covenants set rules for members
steps.text: A new church needed written beliefs and procedures. Section 20, known as the Articles and Covenants, supplied them. Joseph read it at the first conference on 9 June 1830, and members approved it unanimously. Verse 37 sets the conditions for baptism, including a broken heart and a willingness to take Christ’s name. Later verses list duties for elders, priests, teachers, and deacons. Where section 21 named a leader, this document gave members a shared rulebook.

steps.title: Only Joseph may give revelations for the whole Church
steps.text: By September 1830 the new rulebook faced a test. Hiram Page claimed revelations through a stone, and Oliver Cowdery and the Whitmers accepted them. Verse 2 says only Joseph Smith receives commandments and revelations for the Church, “even as Moses.” Verse 11 tells Oliver to tell Page privately that his stone writings are not from the Lord. Verse 13 adds that all things must be done in order and by common consent. The pattern of one revelator and member consent took shape here.

steps.title: Preachers need authority the Church can recognize
steps.text: In February 1831 Joseph Smith had just arrived in Kirtland, Ohio, where many new converts waited for direction. On 9 February twelve elders asked questions, and Joseph dictated what the revelation calls a law. Verse 11 says no one may preach or build up the Church unless ordained by someone with authority. That authority must also be known to the Church. Other verses set moral rules and the consecration of property to the bishop. The question of who speaks for the Church, raised in section 28, now reached every preacher.

steps.title: Priesthood ordinances are tied to the power of godliness
steps.text: Missionaries returning to Kirtland in September 1832 met with Joseph Smith, and this revelation followed. It traces the greater priesthood from Moses back to Adam. Verse 20 says the power of godliness is shown in its ordinances. Verse 21 says that without those ordinances and authority, that power is not shown to people in the flesh. Verses 33–39 describe an oath and covenant for those who receive the priesthood. The authority required in section 42 is here described as more than permission to preach.

steps.title: A high council is formed to settle hard disputes
steps.text: As the Church grew, so did its disputes. On 17 February 1834, twenty-four high priests met at Joseph Smith’s house in Kirtland. They organized a standing high council of twelve high priests. Verse 2 says it would settle serious problems the Church or a bishop’s council could not resolve. Joseph revised the minutes, and the council accepted them as its constitution on 19 February. Leadership was now shared by councils, not only by single officers.

steps.title: Presiding quorums are set side by side
steps.text: In early 1835 the Church organized the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and the first Seventy. Before the Twelve left on a mission in May, Joseph gave them this instruction on priesthood. Verse 22 describes three presiding high priests who form the Presidency of the Church. Verses 23–24 call the Twelve special witnesses, equal in authority to that Presidency. Verse 99 closes the instruction: “let every man learn his duty.” The councils begun in 1834 now formed a full structure of presiding quorums.

guides.title: Zion in Missouri
guides.description: Follow the hope of building Zion in Jackson County, Missouri, from its first mention in 1830 to the delay announced in 1834.

steps.title: Zion’s location is promised but not yet revealed
steps.text: In September 1830 Hiram Page claimed revelations about where Zion would be built. Section 28 answered his claim. Verse 9 says no one yet knows where the city of Zion will be. It adds that the city will be “on the borders by the Lamanites.” Verse 8 sends Oliver Cowdery to preach to American Indians in the West. That mission carried the Zion question toward Missouri.

steps.title: Independence is named the center place
steps.text: Joseph Smith reached Independence, Jackson County, Missouri, on 14 July 1831. He later wrote that he asked when and where Zion would be built. Verse 3 names Independence as the center place and puts a temple lot west of the courthouse. Verse 4 tells the Saints to buy land there and to the west. Other verses assign Sidney Gilbert as agent, Edward Partridge to divide land, and William W. Phelps as printer. The open question of section 28 now had a place on the map.

steps.title: Settlers must act on their own to build Zion
steps.text: Elders arriving in July 1831 found a rough frontier town and few converts. Edward Partridge disagreed with Joseph Smith about the quality of the land being bought. Verse 4 says blessings come “after much tribulation.” Verse 26 says the Lord will not command in all things. Verse 27 says people should do many good things of their own free will. The revelation asked settlers to build Zion by their own effort, not wait for every instruction.

steps.title: Zion requires a willing heart and forgiveness
steps.text: Some who went to Missouri returned to Ohio disappointed. Ezra Booth turned against Joseph Smith, and Partridge had clashed with him over land. On 11 September 1831 this revelation told the elders to forgive one another. Verse 34 says the Lord requires “the heart and a willing mind.” Verse 35 warns that the rebellious will be cut off from the land of Zion. Verse 41 still promises that Zion will flourish. The free effort asked for in section 58 now included forgiving fellow Saints.

steps.title: Zion is defined as the pure in heart
steps.text: By 1833 many Saints lived in Jackson County, and tension with older settlers was rising. On 2 August Joseph dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, about the school in Zion. He did not yet know that a mob had attacked the Saints in Independence in late July. Verses 15–16 command a house in Zion that must be kept undefiled. Verse 21 says, “this is Zion—THE PURE IN HEART.” Verses 25–26 say Zion will escape judgment if she obeys, but not if she does not.

steps.title: Zion is scattered but not moved
steps.text: In November 1833 armed residents drove the Saints out of Jackson County. Most refugees crossed into Clay County, losing homes, goods, and crops. Verse 2 says the Lord allowed the affliction because of the Saints’ transgressions. Verse 6 names contention, envy, and covetous desires among them. Yet verse 17 says Zion will not be moved, though her children are scattered. The warning of section 97 had come true, but the promise of the place remained.

steps.title: Zion’s redemption is postponed
steps.text: In 1834 Joseph Smith led an armed group, later called Zion’s Camp, from Ohio to Missouri. Governor Daniel Dunklin did not call out the militia to restore the Saints to their lands. On 22 June, near Fishing River, Joseph dictated this revelation. Verses 3–4 say the Church did not share with the poor and was not united. Verse 9 tells the elders to wait “for a little season” for the redemption of Zion. Verse 11 says they must first be “endowed with power from on high.” The hope for Zion now waited on the temple being built in Kirtland.

guides.title: Temples from Kirtland to Nauvoo
guides.description: See how revelations moved the Saints from a command to build a house in Kirtland to temple work for the dead in Nauvoo.

steps.title: Elders are commanded to establish a house of God
steps.text: At a conference in Kirtland in late December 1832, elders prayed to learn God’s will about Zion. The long revelation that followed ends with practical commands. Verse 118 tells them to seek learning “by study and also by faith.” Verse 119 tells them to establish a house of prayer, fasting, faith, learning, glory, and order. Joseph Smith sent a copy to Missouri and called it an “olive leaf.” Months would pass before anyone began to build.

steps.title: Delay in building the house is rebuked
steps.text: By June 1833 men had been named to raise funds, but no building had started. Verse 3 calls the neglect “a very grievous sin.” Verse 8 gives the purpose: the Lord would endow the chosen with power from on high in this house. Verse 9 compares this to the apostles waiting at Jerusalem. Verse 15 sets the inner court at fifty-five by sixty-five feet. Work on the Kirtland temple began within days.

steps.title: The dedication prayer asks God to accept the house
steps.text: The Saints worked on the Kirtland temple for nearly three years, often in poverty. On 27 March 1836 Joseph Smith read this prayer to about 1,000 people at its dedication. The official heading says the prayer was given by revelation. Verse 12 asks that God’s glory rest on the house and his presence remain there. Verse 13 asks that all who enter may feel his power. The prayer asks God to fulfill the endowment promised in section 95.

steps.title: Joseph and Oliver report the Lord accepting the temple
steps.text: One week later, on Easter Sunday, 3 April 1836, Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery prayed behind veils at the pulpit. A scribe recorded their account in Joseph’s journal. They report seeing the Lord standing on the pulpit. In verse 7 he says, “I have accepted this house.” Verse 8 adds a condition: the people must not pollute it. The account presents this as the answer to the dedication prayer.

steps.title: Elijah is reported to bring keys about fathers and children
steps.text: The same account continues with three more visitors. Moses gives keys of gathering Israel, and Elias gives the dispensation of the gospel of Abraham. Then, in verses 13–14, Elijah appears and says Malachi’s promised time has fully come. Verse 15 names the work: turning the hearts of fathers and children to each other. The account gives no details yet about how that turning would happen. Joseph would later tie this promise to ordinances for the dead in Nauvoo.

steps.title: Nauvoo must build a temple for baptisms for the dead
steps.text: By 1839 the Saints had left Kirtland and Missouri and settled at Commerce, Illinois, later named Nauvoo. Joseph Smith began teaching baptism for the dead there in 1840. On 19 January 1841 this revelation commanded a new temple. Verses 29–30 say baptism for the dead belongs in the Lord’s house. Verse 31 accepts baptisms elsewhere only for a set time while the temple is built. Verse 32 warns of rejection, with their dead, if the Saints fail to build.

steps.title: Records weld the living and the dead together
steps.text: In September 1842 Joseph Smith was hiding from officers seeking his arrest. From hiding he wrote letters to the Church about recording baptisms for the dead. Verse 17 quotes Malachi’s promise about Elijah, which section 110 reported fulfilled. Verse 18 says there must be a “welding link” between fathers and children, and names baptism for the dead. Verse 24 asks the Saints to present a book of their dead in the finished temple. Joseph was killed in 1844, before the Nauvoo temple was finished. Its purpose had grown from endowing missionaries to joining families across generations.

guides.title: From Liberty Jail to the West
guides.description: Follow the Saints from Joseph Smith’s imprisonment in Missouri through Nauvoo and his death to the trek west in 1847.

steps.title: A prisoner’s cry receives a reply of peace
steps.text: After the 1838 conflict in Missouri, Governor Lilburn Boggs ordered the Saints out of the state. Joseph Smith and others were held in the jail at Liberty from 1 December 1838. In March 1839 Joseph wrote to the Church from there. Verse 1 asks, “O God, where art thou?” Verse 7 answers, “My son, peace be unto thy soul,” and calls his trouble “but a small moment.” The tour begins at the low point of the Church’s Missouri years.

steps.title: Suffering is said to give experience
steps.text: A second letter, dated about 22 March, continues in the same voice. Verse 6 pictures Joseph’s six-year-old son clinging to him and asking why he cannot stay. Verse 7 lists trials up to a sentence of death. It says “all these things shall give thee experience, and shall be for thy good.” Verse 8 adds that the Son of Man has descended below them all. Section 121 promised the trial would be short; this text says it could also teach.

steps.title: Priesthood power is limited to persuasion and love
steps.text: The same letters also look at how leaders use power. Verse 37 warns that heaven withdraws when someone uses priesthood to cover sins or compel others. Verse 41 says priesthood influence rests only on persuasion, long-suffering, gentleness, meekness, and unfeigned love. Verse 46 promises a dominion that flows “without compulsory means.” Joseph wrote this while held by force himself. The prison letters address both the Saints’ suffering and their own conduct.

steps.title: Nauvoo begins again after Missouri
steps.text: In April 1839 Joseph left custody during a transfer and joined the Saints in Illinois. They built a new city at Nauvoo on the Mississippi River. On 19 January 1841 this revelation addressed the failure in Missouri. Verse 49 says that when enemies hinder a commanded work, the Lord accepts the offering instead. Verse 51 applies this to those hindered in Jackson County. Verse 55 then commands the Saints to build a house again in Nauvoo.

steps.title: Joseph and Hyrum Smith are killed at Carthage
steps.text: In June 1844 the Nauvoo city council had an opposition press destroyed. Joseph and Hyrum Smith were jailed at Carthage, Illinois, and a mob shot them there on 27 June. John Taylor was wounded, and Willard Richards escaped unhurt. Section 135 is not a revelation but a tribute, traditionally attributed to John Taylor. Verse 3 lists Joseph’s work and says he sealed his mission with his own blood. It was placed at the end of the 1844 Doctrine and Covenants.

steps.title: The westward camp is organized by covenant
steps.text: Conflict continued, and most Saints left Nauvoo in 1846 and wintered on the Missouri River. Brigham Young, leading as President of the Twelve, gave this revelation at Winter Quarters on 14 January 1847. Verse 2 organizes the people into companies with a covenant to keep the commandments. Verse 3 places captains of hundreds, fifties, and tens under the Twelve Apostles. Other verses tell the companies to care for the poor and widows. The exodus was planned as an organized march, not a scattered flight.

steps.title: Joseph’s death is placed within the story
steps.text: Section 136 also looks back on the losses since Liberty Jail. Verse 31 says the people must be tried in all things to prepare for the glory of Zion. Verse 38 says Joseph laid the foundation and was faithful. Verse 39 says his death was needed to seal his testimony with his blood. This echoes the language of section 135. In July 1847 the first company reached the Salt Lake Valley.

guides.title: Revelations about life after death
guides.description: Trace how revelations from 1832 to 1918 described the kingdoms of glory, the judgment of the dead, and their redemption.

steps.title: Joseph and Sidney report a vision of the Son
steps.text: On 16 February 1832 Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon were revising the Bible in Hiram, Ohio. Joseph had reasoned that heaven must hold more than one kingdom if people are judged by their deeds. While pondering John 5:29, the two reported a shared vision. Verse 22 gives their testimony of Christ: “That he lives!” Verse 24 says the worlds were created through him. Their account of the afterlife begins with this claim about Christ.

steps.title: Heaven is described as three kingdoms of glory
steps.text: The vision divides the resurrected into three glories. Verse 70 compares the celestial glory to the sun, “the highest of all.” Verse 71 compares the terrestrial to the moon, and verse 81 compares the telestial to the stars. Verse 109 says the telestial inhabitants are as countless as the stars. Only the sons of perdition are left outside these kingdoms. This differed sharply from the common Protestant teaching of one heaven and one hell. Some early members found it hard to accept.

steps.title: Those who died without the gospel are not shut out
steps.text: Section 76 left a question about people who never heard the gospel. On 21 January 1836 leaders met in the unfinished Kirtland temple to prepare for its dedication. Joseph reported a vision of the celestial kingdom. He saw his brother Alvin, who died in 1823 without baptism, and wondered how he was there. Verse 7 says those who would have received the gospel will be heirs of that kingdom. Verse 9 says the Lord judges by works and by “the desire of their hearts.”

steps.title: The living and the dead need each other
steps.text: By 1840 Joseph Smith was teaching baptism for the dead in Nauvoo, Illinois. In September 1842 he wrote letters giving rules for recording these baptisms. Verse 15 says the salvation of the dead is “necessary and essential to our salvation.” Echoing Paul, it says they cannot be made perfect without us, nor we without them. Verse 18 calls the ordinance a “welding link” between fathers and children. The hope given for Alvin in section 137 now came with an ordinance the living could perform.

steps.title: Marriage is tied to the highest degree of glory
steps.text: In May 1843 Joseph Smith taught at the Johnson home in Ramus, Illinois. William Clayton recorded these teachings, which were later combined as section 131. Verse 1 says the celestial glory has three degrees. Verse 2 says the highest requires the new and everlasting covenant of marriage. At the time, Joseph was privately teaching eternal and plural marriage to a small circle. Verse 7 adds that all spirit is matter, too fine to be seen now. The afterlife was now described in terms of families as well as individuals.

steps.title: Christ is seen organizing messengers among the dead
steps.text: In 1918 Church President Joseph F. Smith was pondering 1 Peter 3 and 4 in Salt Lake City. That year had brought world war, a deadly influenza outbreak, and the death of his son Hyrum. On 3 October he reported a vision of the world of spirits. Verse 29 says Christ did not go in person to the wicked. Verse 30 says he organized righteous spirits as messengers to teach all the dead. Verse 33 lists what they taught, including vicarious baptism. The vision describes how the dead learn the gospel that section 128 asked the living to help with.

steps.title: Redemption of the dead is joined to temple ordinances
steps.text: The vision closes by linking the spirit world to the work of the living. Verse 57 says faithful elders keep preaching after they die. Verse 58 says the dead who repent will be redeemed through the ordinances of the house of God. Church leaders accepted the account unanimously on 31 October 1918. It became section 138 of the Doctrine and Covenants in 1981. The line from section 76 ends here with a plan for teaching all the dead.
